INTRODUCTION 1


OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
1-4
Situated at the northwest corner of San Diego 
County, along the Pacific Ocean, the City of 
Oceanside is a unique coastal community 
endowed with a rich history, a beautiful natural 
setting, a diverse population, a host of waterfront 
amenities, an array of distinct neighborhoods, and 
a growing and increasingly diverse local economy. 
Bounded by Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, 
the cities of Vista and Carlsbad, and the unincor-
porated communities of Fallbrook and Bonsall, 
the City’s 42 square miles of land area include 
character-defining built environments, farmland, 
natural landforms, watercourses, riparian areas, 
and upland habitats. 
With a population of more than 175,000 residents, 
Oceanside is the third most populous city in the 
San Diego region. Housing growth has significant-
ly outpaced employment growth in Oceanside, 
resulting in a comparatively low jobs-to-housing 
ratio. However, over the past two decades, a 
large employment hub comprised of several light 
industrial parks has emerged in central portions 
of the City, providing high-quality jobs in a range 
of economic sectors. At the same time, the City 
has significantly expanded its hospitality sector, 
becoming a popular visitor destination.
After decades of suburban expansion into inland 
areas – i.e., the San Luis Rey Valley, the Oceanside 
Boulevard corridor, and the Highway 78 corridor – 
Oceanside must now provide for growth through 
more efficient use of land within the City’s already 
urbanized areas. In so doing, the City can revital-
ize its major commercial corridors, expand mobil-
ity options, and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions while preserving natural resources, 
farmland, and the City’s exceptional vistas of sur-
rounding open spaces.
For the first time in its 135-year history, the City of 
Oceanside has prepared a comprehensive update 
of its General Plan, addressing all state-mandat-
ed topic areas as well as other matters of interest 
to community members. The General Plan (Plan) 
outlines the City’s vision for its future – one that 
reflects the values and priorities of community 
members and provides a blueprint for positive 
change. In keeping with this vision, the Plan pro-
motes responsible growth that supports quality of 
life, environmental quality, economic prosperity, 
and social equity. The Plan identifies what makes 
Oceanside a unique community – in terms of its 
assets, opportunities, and challenges – and out-
lines goals, policies, and actions that seek to pre-
serve and enhance the City’s positive attributes 
while attenuating conditions that work against 
fulfillment of the City’s vision. 
This introductory chapter outlines the Vision and 
Guiding Principles that have helped to shape the 
Plan. It also introduces the Plan’s purpose, use, 
and structure, and how it can be amended and 
updated to adapt to changing circumstances. The 
Photo credit: Terry Brown


1-5
INTRODUCTION 1
chapters that follow are organized around themes 
that provide a framework for accommodating 
growth and change, conserving essential resourc-
es, and enhancing community character in ways 
that align with the Vision and Guiding Principles. 
The General Plan was developed through exten-
sive community engagement utilizing an array of 
tools and activities, including in-person and virtu-
al workshops, meetings with individual stakehold-
ers and small groups, open house events, forums 
with subject matter experts, surveys, videos, and 
email and social media communications deployed 
at various stages of the planning process. 
Together, these tools and activities engaged over 
two thousand community members and generat-
ed thousands of responses. These responses have 
informed the planning process and contributed 
to the development of the Vision and Guiding 
Principles. 
Throughout the community engagement pro-
cess, the City Council, the Planning Commission, 
and several advisory groups received updates on 
this process and, in turn, provided input on the 
evolving Plan. By adopting the General Plan, the 
City Council affirmed the Vision and Guiding 
Principles and committed the City to pursuing 
their implementation. 
The General Plan is comprehensive and long-range 
and will be used on an ongoing basis to direct the 
City’s decision making, reflecting the City’s com-
mitment to the ideals set forth herein. All future 
actions related to land use, urban design, mobility, 
conservation, community facilities and services, 
mitigation of natural and human-induced hazards, 
and other topics addressed in the General Plan 
should be consistent with all components of this 
document. 
The General Plan has been prepared in consulta-
tion with staff from all City disciplines – i.e., the 
City Manager’s Office, Development Services, 
Public Works, Neighborhood Services, Parks 
and 
Recreation, 
Water 
Utilities, 
Economic 
Development, the Fire Department, and the Police 
Department. It is anticipated that the General Plan 
will serve to guide investment and actions for all of 
these disciplines, while supporting interdisciplinary 
coordination and providing for a whole-of-govern-
ment approach to key issues and challenges.


OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
1-6
1.1 Oceanside Setting 
and Regional 
Context
An important gateway into the San Diego met-
ropolitan area, the City of Oceanside links the 
North County Coastal subregion with the inland 
cities of Vista, San Marcos, and Escondido, as well 
as portions of unincorporated San Diego County. 
While Oceanside’s physical characteristics bear 
many similarities to the neighboring coastal 
cities of Carlsbad, Encinitas, Solana Beach, and 
Del Mar, the City’s socioeconomic profile more 
closely resembles those of its inland neighbors. 
Consequently, Oceanside is viewed by many as 
the region’s most accessible, welcoming, and 
down-to-earth coastal community.
As shown in Figure 6-1, Interstate 5 connects 
Oceanside with other California coastal cities to 
the north and south.  Highways 76 and 78 tra-
verse the City in a generally east-west direction, 
linking the coast to the Interstate 15 corridor. The 
historic Coast Highway parallels Interstate 5 and 
links the City to the neighboring City of Carlsbad 
to the south. 
Oceanside offers more than three miles of beach-
es, the only pier and harbor in the North County 
coastal area, major recreational amenities such 
as Guajome Regional Park, Mission San Luis Rey 
(the largest mission in California), the California 
Surf Museum, the Oceanside Museum of Art, El 
Corazon Park, events such as surfing competitions 
and youth soccer tournaments, and markets and 
festivals. Oceanside is somewhat unique among 
southern California coastal cities in maintaining 
nearly 3,500 acres of farmland, located in the 
City’s northeast corner in the South Morro Hills 
neighborhood. 
Bounded by the Pacific Ocean to the west, Marine 
Corps Base Camp Pendleton to the north, and 
unincorporated rural areas to the east, Oceanside’s 
peripheral location within the San Diego region 
has historically presented challenges to economic 
development. However, in recent years the City 
has seen employment gains in hospitality, sports 
equipment and apparel, bio-technology, and other 
sectors. 
Oceanside is an important gateway to the San 
Diego region, as well as a major transit hub. The 
Oceanside Transit Center accommodates four rail 
services that connect the City to Orange County, 
Downtown San Diego, and other cities within the 
Highway 78 Corridor. Rail service is supplement-
ed by bus service operated by the North County 
Transit District (NCTD).
The City’s coastal assets, cultural venues, restau-
rant and micro-brewing scene, and linkages to 
other parts of southern California make it an 
increasingly popular visitor destination.

1.2 Planning Area
The General Plan Planning Area (Planning Area), 
as shown in Figure 1-2, encompasses the area 
addressed by the General Plan Update. The 
Planning Area includes Oceanside and its Sphere 
of Influence (SOI) – an area outside of the City 
limits designated by the San Diego Local Agency 
Formation Commission (LAFCO) as the City’s 
probable future boundary and service area. The 
Planning Area encompasses 27,012 acres (or 
approximately 42 square miles). The City’s SOI 
is relatively small—about 20 acres—and presents 
few opportunities for additional development. 
The City’s population as July 1, 2022 was estimat-
ed at 172,199 by the US Census, a slight decline 
from 174,068 in 2020, paralleling trends across 
the state. 
The Planning Area is bordered by the Marine 
Corps Base, Camp Pendleton to the north, the 
unincorporated rural communities of Fallbrook 
and Bonsall to the northeast, the City of Vista 
to the southeast, and the City of Carlsbad to the 
south. The Planning Area’s southwestern border 
includes three miles of Pacific Ocean coastline. 
The lower San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta Creek, 
and Buena Vista Creek flow in a westerly direc-
tion through the Planning Area and drain into the 
Pacific Ocean. These waterbodies flow through 
alluvial areas bounded by hillsides and mesas, 
essentially dividing Oceanside into three distinct 
east-west corridors.
A portion of the Planning Area is within the state’s 
Coastal Zone. Land uses in this area are governed 
by the Local Coastal Program (LCP) and Land Use 
Plan, which is certified by the California Coastal 
Commission. The LCP effectively supplants the 
General Plan as the governing land use policy 
document for the City’s Coastal Zone. As shown 
in Figure 1-2, the City’s coastal zone lies primar-
ily between the coastline and the inland side of 
Coast Highway, with inland extensions along the 
City’s east-west waterways.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
1-10
(e.g., Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element, 
Integrated Mobility Element). The CAP has also 
been updated in parallel with the General Plan, to 
address both the state’s new mandates relating to 
greenhouse gases (GHG) reduction and communi-
ty priorities regarding economic growth, employ-
ment opportunities, workforce training, social 
equity, etc. 
The General Plan identifies and addresses current 
and future opportunities and challenges, state 
law, regional priorities, and best practices and 
approaches in urban planning, economic devel-
opment, climate action, and other key topics that 
have emerged in recent years.
The General Plan serves several purposes:
• Establishing a long-range vision that reflects the 
aspirations of the community and outlines steps 
to achieve this vision
• Outlining long-range development policies 
that will guide City departments, Planning 
Commission, and City Council decision-making;
• Providing a basis for judging whether specific 
development proposals and public projects are 
in harmony with plan policies;
• Planning in a manner that meets future land 
needs based on the projected population and job 
growth;
• Allowing City departments, other public 
agencies, and private developers to design 
projects that will enhance the character of the 
community, preserve environmental resources, 
and minimize hazards; and
• Providing the basis for establishing and setting 
priorities for detailed plans and implementing 
programs, such as the Zoning Ordinance, 
subdivision regulations, specific and master 
plans, and the Capital Improvement Program. 
Due to the general and long-range nature of the 
General Plan, there will be instances where more 
detailed studies will be necessary in order to 
implement the Plan’s policies.
1.3 Purpose and Scope 
of the General Plan
California Government Code Section 65300 
requires each city and county in California to 
adopt a General Plan “for the physical develop-
ment of the county or city, and any land outside its 
boundaries which…bears relation to its planning.” 
The Oceanside General Plan establishes the City’s 
overall approach to growth and change within its 
boundaries to the year 2050, containing both a 
statement of the community’s vision of its long-
term development as well as the goals, policies, 
and actions to support that vision and guide the 
physical growth of the City. The Plan contains pol-
icies to inform decision-making related to devel-
opment, housing, transportation, environmental 
quality, natural and human induced hazards, com-
munity facilities and services, parks, and open 
spaces.
The City of Oceanside has chosen to take a 
phased approach to the comprehensive General 
Plan Update process. In 2019, the City Council 
adopted the Economic Development Element 
(EDE), Energy and Climate Action Element (ECAE), 
and Climate Action Plan (CAP) as part of Phase 1 
of the General Plan update. These new compo-
nents of the City’s General Plan provide import-
ant policy direction for Phase is project, which 
includes the updating of all of the City’s remaining 
General Plan elements. These elements address 
the topics of land use, circulation, housing, con-
servation and open space, community facilities, 
safety, and noise. The titles of the updated ele-
ments not only identify these topics but also 
reflect the City’s fundamental approach to them

INTRODUCTION 1
GENERAL PLAN REQUIREMENTS
California grants local authorities power over land 
use decisions. As a result, cities have considerable 
flexibility in preparing their general plans as long 
as state requirements are met. The California 
Government Code establishes both the content 
of general plans and rules for their adoption and 
subsequent amendment. Together, state law and 
judicial decisions establish three overall guide-
lines for general plans:
• Comprehensive. This requirement has two 
aspects. First, the general plan must be 
geographically comprehensive. That is, it must 
apply throughout the entire incorporated area 
as well as other areas the City deems relevant 
to its planning. Second, the general plan must 
address the full range of issues that affect the 
City’s physical development.
• Internally Consistent. This requirement states 
that the general plan must fully integrate its 
separate parts and relate them to each other 
without conflict. “Horizontal” consistency 
applies as much to figures and diagrams as to 
the general plan text. It also applies to data and 
analysis as well as policies. All adopted portions 
of the general plan, whether required by state 
law or not, have equal legal weight. None may 
supersede another, so the general plan must 
avoid conflicts among the provisions of each 
element.
• Long-Range. Because anticipated development 
will affect the City and the people who live 
or work there for years to come, State law 
requires every general plan to take a long-term 
perspective. This General Plan uses the year 
2050 as its planning horizon.
The state mandates that all general plans address 
at least seven topics: land use, circulation, hous-
ing, conservation, open space, noise, and safety. 
Recently, the state has established a requirement 
that, for cities and counties with state-defined 
“disadvantaged 
communities,” 
environmental 
justice should be addressed in the general plan, 
either in a standalone element or integrated with 
other elements. The Environmental Protection 
Agency (EPA) defines environmental justice as 
“the fair treatment and meaningful involvement 
of all people regardless of race, color, nation-
al origin, or income, with respect to the devel-
opment, implementation, and enforcement of 
environmental laws, regulations, and policies.” 
While there are no state-defined disadvantaged 
communities in Oceanside, the City recognizes 
environmental justice as an important concern 
and has thus chosen to address it throughout the 
General Plan. The City understands that even 
though there are no local communities that meet 
the state definition of “disadvantaged,” there are 
historically under-resourced areas in Oceanside 
where residents continue to face economic inse-
curity, linguistic isolation, exposure to pollution, 
and other challenges.
Beyond the state-mandated general plan topics, 
local governments may address optional topics 
in their general plans. Examples of topics local 
governments choose to address include air quality, 
public health, sustainability, community design, 
community facilities, economic development, 
energy, and agriculture, and recreational facilities. 
All general plan topics, regardless of whether they 
are mandatory or optional, must be consistent with 
one another. No element is legally subordinate to 
another.1
1  State of California Government Code Sections 65302 and

The Oceanside General Plan is presented in seven 
elements, organized around both state-mandated 
and optional topics or themes, plus the separate-
ly-bound Housing Element.
Housing elements are required by state law to 
be updated more frequently than the rest of the 
General Plan and are typically published as sep-
arate documents to facilitate easier updating 
according to the state-defined housing cycles. 
Unlike the other mandatory general plan ele-
ments, the housing element is subject to detailed 
statutory requirements and mandatory review by 
the state of California Department of Housing 
and Community Development (HCD). The City’s 
2023-2041 Housing Element has been certified 
by the state HCD.
65300.5

the City’s Housing Element addresses Oceanside’s 
housing needs by identifying land resources avail-
able for housing development, acknowledging 
constraints to the provision of new and affordable 
housing, and establishing a variety of housing-re-
lated programs. 
The General Plan is thematically organized and 
includes all of the topics required under state 
law, as well as additional topics of local impor-
tance – climate change and sustainability, historic 
and cultural resources, community design, and 
public health and equity. Table 1-1 shows corre-
spondence between state-required elements and 
where these are included in the General Plan’s 
thematic elements.

1.4 Community 
Engagement and 
the Planning Process
Oceanside’s General Plan represents a culmina-
tion of extensive efforts to understand existing 
conditions, identify constraints and opportuni-
ties, and chart Oceanside’s future through com-
munity engagement, fieldwork, technical study, 
analysis of state and regional priorities, and col-
laboration across City disciplines. These efforts 
have revealed key community assets, opportuni-
ties for positive change, challenges that must be 
overcome, and a wide range of community values, 
priorities, and concerns. 
Community input was gathered through a variety 
of methods to achieve a broad understanding of 
the community’s vision for its future. Community 
input was systematically documented and made 
available through a project website developed for 
the General Plan process. 
In addition to community engagement, four 
in-depth background reports and technical analy-
ses provided a foundation for under¬standing both 
the challenges and opportunities that Oceanside 
faces. Additionally, the documents adopted in 
the first phase of the City’s General Plan Update 
(EDE, ECAE, and CAP) provide important direc-
tion for this second phase, including policies that 
call for economic diversity, sub-regional collabo-
ration, smart growth, sustainable building design, 
and renewable energy procurement. 
State legislation and guidelines on housing, farm-
land preservation, GHG reduction, climate adap-
tation, and environmental justice are reflected 
in the updated General Plan and companion 
planning documents. The General Plan furthers 
the state’s efforts to promote sustainable devel-
opment, expand housing opportunities, pro-
tect natural resources, and reduce vehicle miles 
traveled (VMT). Additional information on state 
priorities can be found on the webpages for 
the California Office of Planning and Research 
and the California Department of Housing and 
Community Development. 
Regional planning priorities such as smart growth, 
expanded mobility options, shoreline manage-
ment, military base access, and electric vehicle 
charging infrastructure also provide valuable 
direction to the local planning process. The City 
has an important role in implementing these 
regional priorities. At the same time, the City 
must advocate for its own interests as part of 
its participation in the regional planning process, 
particularly with respect to investments in trans-
portation infrastructure.
The following pages elaborate on the outreach, 
research, and relevant planning efforts that have 
contributed to the development of Oceanside’s 
Vision Statement.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
1-16
1.5 Community Vision 
and Guiding 
Principles
The Community Vision and Guiding Principles 
provide the basis for the goals, policies, and 
actions outlined in the General Plan and associat-
ed planning documents. Informed by community 
values, the Vision presents an aspirational view 
of the City’s evolution through the planning hori-
zon of 2050. The Guiding Principles contribute to 
the structure of the General Plan, identifying the 
topics that the plan will address in the greatest 
detail. For more detail on the Vision and Guiding 
Principles, see the project website.
COMMUNITY VISION
The Community Vision reads as follows: 
Oceanside will leverage its many assets – including 
its human capital – to promote quality of life, eco-
nomic prosperity, environmental quality, and social 
equity. The City will grow and diversify the local 
economy, foster safe and vibrant public spaces, pro-
tect the natural environment, conserve farmland, 
and provide high-quality community facilities and 
services. The City will balance economic, environ-
mental, and social priorities in a manner that pro-
motes Oceanside’s long-term sustainability and resil-
ience. The benefits of this conscientious approach to 
the City’s future will be shared by all members of the 
Oceanside community.
Housing and employment growth will be concen-
trated within already urbanized areas, with a par-
ticular focus on creating vibrant, walkable, visually 
appealing, and engaging mixed-use districts centered 
along Coast Highway, within the major east-west 
commercial corridors, around Sprinter stations, and 
in the Downtown District. This focus on infill and 
redevelopment will allow for the preservation and 
enhancement of recreational open space, sensitive 
habitat, and existing single-family neighborhoods. 
Concurrently, strategic planning emphasizing agri-
tourism, clustered housing, rural design standards, 
view 
preservation, 
and 
limited 
infrastructure 
improvements will help preserve the agricultural 
heritage and character of South Morro Hills, one of 
San Diego County’s last remaining active agricultural 
areas west of Interstate 15.
An inviting and well-maintained public realm will 
enhance Oceanside’s visual quality and provide 
safe and comfortable spaces for residents to shop, 
gather, enjoy the outdoors, and build communi-
ty. Neighborhoods will transition seamlessly from 
low-density residential areas to higher-intensity 
mixed-use corridors, improving multimodal con-
nectivity while preserving each neighborhood’s 
unique character and significant historic and cultural 
resources. An enhanced network of bike and pedes-
trian trails, centered along the coastline, the San Luis 
River, and other waterways, will connect destinations, 
provide recreational opportunities, and improve traf-
fic safety throughout the City. This “smart growth” 
approach will promote walkability, transit use, neigh-
borhood access to everyday services and amenities, 
Photo credit: Terry Brown


1-17
INTRODUCTION 1
and urban design elements that promote a sense of 
place, social interaction, and natural surveillance of 
the public realm.
Oceanside will preserve and enhance the ecologi-
cal, scenic, and recreational values of its coastline, 
riparian areas, hillsides, and open spaces, ensuring 
that these resources are available to all Oceansiders 
for generations to come. Consistent with the City’s 
adopted Energy and Climate Action Element and 
Climate Action Plan, the City will work diligently to 
reduce its carbon footprint, while building resilience 
to climate change. Climate mitigation and adaptation 
strategies include renewable energy procurement, 
reduced vehicles miles traveled (VMT), expanded 
tree canopy, “green infrastructure,” and community 
preparedness and responsiveness to climate-exacer-
bated threats and hazards such wildfires, flooding, 
and drought.
The Oceanside community will foster social and eco-
nomic diversity and provide all residents with ready 
access to City resources. New and rehabilitated hous-
ing developments will serve all income levels, includ-
ing low and very low-income households, ensuring 
that all Oceansiders have a safe and affordable place 
to call home. Oceanside will continue to embrace 
and celebrate its diversity through programs and 
community events, support of educational and cul-
tural institutions, inclusive community outreach, and 
a commitment to environmental justice and social 
equity. This includes efforts to ensure that historical-
ly disadvantaged communities are not disproportion-
ately impacted by pollution, noise, traffic, or other 
threats to public health, economic opportunity, and 
quality of life. 
The City will continue to honor its Native American 
heritage, highlighting Oceanside’s rich history 
of Native American settlement, protecting tribal 
resources, and maintaining constructive dialogue 
with the San Luis Rey Band of Mission Indians and 
other tribal groups in the region.
In partnership with local groups and institutions, the 
City will assert its role in charting the future of the 
San Diego region, working closely with neighboring 
jurisdictions to address shared concerns and seek 
mutual benefits, participating actively in regional 
planning efforts, and implementing complementary 
state priorities and regional policies at the local level.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
1-20
1.6 Related Documents
GENERAL PLAN UPDATE, PHASE 1
Economic Development Element 
(EDE)
The EDE was adopted in 2019 and informs future 
actions affecting the City’s fiscal resources and the 
local economy. The overarching goal of the EDE is 
to grow and diversify the City’s economy in ways 
that lift the fortunes and enhance the wellbeing of 
all Oceanside residents. Goals and policies in the 
EDE will enhance quality of life; promote econom-
ic prosperity; make Oceanside more economically 
resilient; and strengthen collaborative partner-
ships between the City, educational institutions, 
business groups, and neighboring cities.
Energy and Climate Action Element 
(ECAE)
Prepared in conjunction with the EDE and also 
adopted in 2019, the ECAE focuses on the City’s 
responsibility to reduce its carbon footprint in a 
manner consistent with the state’s greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets. The ECAE 
also addresses environmental sustainability more 
broadly, promulgating goals and policies that 
encourage cleaner, healthier, and less resource-in-
tensive consumer choices and business practices. 
The ECAE encourages smart growth, alternative 
transportation, solid waste diversion, water con-
servation and local water harvesting, urban for-
estry, and the preservation of local agriculture. 
The fundamental goal of the ECAE is to reduce 
reliance on fossil fuels and move the City toward 
a carbon-neutral future.
SMART AND SUSTAINABLE 
CORRIDORS SPECIFIC PLAN
Concurrent with the General Plan Update, 
the City prepared the Smart and Sustainable 
Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), a focused reg-
ulatory plan covering the three main east-west 
corridors—Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, 
and Vista Way. The SSCSP establishes the zoning 
for these corridors, with form-based design stan-
dards that promote high-quality development. 
The SSCSP envisions the three corridors as 
walkable, visually cohesive, tree-lined boulevards 
that foster a strong sense of place and community 
identity. Mixed-use development in these corri-
dors will accommodate much of the City’s housing 
and employment growth over the planning hori-
zon, while creating synergies between residential 
and non-residential uses and providing for more 
natural surveillance. The SSCSP is covered by the 
same EIR as the General Plan and was adopted 
concurrently.
CLIMATE ACTION PLAN (CAP)
The CAP has been updated concurrently with 
the General Plan to ensure consistency with the 
updated growth scenarios presented in the Plan. 
The CAP forecasts future GHG emissions from 
a range of sources, establishes emissions reduc-
tion targets consistent with California’s goal of 
achieving carbon neutrality by 2045, and outlines 
a broad range of strategies designed to reduce the 
City’s carbon footprint.
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT 
REPORT
The General Plan is accompanied by an EIR, 
prepared in accordance with the California 
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The EIR also 
serves as the EIR on the SSCSP and the CAP. The 
EIR is a detailed analysis of the potential environ-
mental effects of the General Plan/SSCSP/CAP, 
evaluating alternatives and presenting ways to 
reduce or avoid environmental damage. The EIR 
process has also informed policies that mitigate 
potentially adverse environmental effects of the 
Plan, thus resulting in a largely “self-mitigating” 
Plan.
EXISTING CONDITIONS REPORTS
As a part of the General Plan Update process, four 
existing conditions reports were produced to pro-
vide technical analysis and planning context on a 
range of topics relevant to the General Plan:
• Background Report 1: Market Analysis
• Background Report 2: Land Use and Community 
Resources
• Background Report 3: Mobility
• Background Report 4: Environmental Resources

INTRODUCTION 1
OTHER RELEVANT PLANNING 
DOCUMENTS
Local Coastal Program
Oceanside’s Local Coastal Program (LCP) is a plan-
ning document that regulates development in the 
City’s Coastal Zone and establishes a long-range 
vision for the community. The California Coastal 
Act, passed in 1976, provides for coastal jurisdic-
tions to adopt a Local Coastal Program to ensure 
local implementation of Coastal Act priorities. 
The City is currently updating its Local Coastal 
Program, originally adopted in 1986, to address 
the changing issues that the City is facing in its 
Coastal Zone, including the threat of sea level rise, 
increasing visitor traffic, more stringent water 
quality and habitat management requirements, 
and aging infrastructure.
Coast Highway Vision and Strategic 
Plan
In 2009, the City of Oceanside adopted the 
Coast Highway Vision and Strategic Plan. This 
plan serves as a blueprint for the revitalization 
and enhancement of the Coast Highway corridor 
between Harbor Drive in the north and Buena 
Vista Lagoon in the south. The Vision and Strategic 
Plan includes several recommendations to trans-
form Coast Highway from an auto-oriented thor-
oughfare into a “complete street” that serves all 
modes of transportation from automobiles to 
pedestrians to bicyclists and transit vehicles.
Downtown – Article 12 Amendment
In 2020 the City Council adopted an amend-
ment to Article 12 in the City’s Zoning Ordinance 
that regulates development in the Downtown. 
The updated Downtown Zoning Ordinance not 
only allows for more commercial uses, which 
are currently allowed in other parts of the City, 
within the downtown area, but also implements 
a streamlined review of some commercial uses 
in the downtown area through an administrative 
conditional use permit (ACUP) process or by per-
mitting the use by right. This update to Article 12 
is the latest move in the City’s effort to revitalize 
the Downtown and encourage new development 
in the area.
Parks and Recreation Master Plan
In 2019, the City adopted a new Parks and 
Recreation Master Plan (Master Plan). The Master 
Plan provides a guide for the orderly development 
of future park, recreation, and open space facili-
ties and programs in order to meet the communi-
ty’s current and future needs. The Master Plan is 
intended to provide a realistic view of the City’s 
parks and recreation system and to develop a 
vision for the parks and recreation system through 
2030. The General Plan builds on the work done 
in the Parks Master Plan to present a comprehen-
sive view of City’s parks and recreation resources 
through the 2050 planning horizon. The General 
Plan growth projections and locations for new 
residential development would need to be reflect-
ed in the next update of the Master Plan.

1.7 General Plan 
Administration 
IMPLEMENTATION
General Plan policies are action-oriented and 
serve as the implementation plan for the General 
Plan. The General Plan is implemented through 
the Zoning and the Subdivision ordinances, 
review of development applications, decisions of 
the Planning Commission and the City Council, 
specific plans, and the City’s Capital Improvement 
Program (CIP). The Zoning Ordinance includes 
detailed use classifications and standards. The 
zoning map must be consistent with the General 
Plan map, but it will not be identical to it. Specific 
plans and the CIP also must be consistent with the 
General Plan. 
AMENDMENTS TO THE GENERAL 
PLAN 
The General Plan is a living document. As such, 
it should be updated periodically as specific cir-
cumstances change from the time of writing, to 
respond to new state or federal laws, or to modify 
policies that may become obsolete or unrealistic 
over time. 
Changes in policy as well as the development of 
unforeseen opportunities or needs will require 
amendment of the General Plan. Per California 
Government Code Section 65358, no mandato-
ry element of this General Plan may be amended 
more frequently than four times during any cal-
endar year. Within this limitation, amendments 
may be made at any time as determined by the 
Oceanside City Council, and each amendment 
may include more than one change to the Plan.

Oceanside will leverage its many assets to promote quality of 
life, economic development, and environmental quality. The 
City will distinguish itself and burnish its brand by preserving 
and enhancing its cultural, historical, and recreational resources, 
unique neighborhoods, and one-of-a-kind destinations. Infill 
and redevelopment in commercial corridors will provide 
for high-quality urban design and a strong sense of place.  
Meanwhile, the functional and visual integrity of established 
single-family neighborhoods will be protected and improved.

2.1 Background
All local communities are remarkable in their own 
way, and this fact is very much in evidence in the 
City of Oceanside. With a diverse population, a 
variety of distinctive natural features, several 
unique coastal amenities, an eclectic built envi-
ronment, and a rich history that includes Native 
American settlement, Spanish and Mexican rule, 
agriculture, railroads, and an 80-year relation-
ship with Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, 
Oceanside distinguishes itself from other commu-
nities in a multitude of ways.  
The Remarkable Community Element (RC) cele-
brates and seeks to preserve and enhance those 
characteristics that contribute to Oceanside’s 
uniqueness and positive brand. The RC also 
acknowledges and considers ways to improve 
upon conditions that detract from quality of life, 
create or perpetuate inequities, inhibit econom-
ic development, and diminish community pride. 
The RC reflects the desire of the community to 
not only maintain (and, in some cases, adapt) 
the distinctive qualities of Oceanside in the face 
of inevitable change but also embrace changes 
that are in the City’s best interests. To this end, 
the RC acknowledges the City’s dynamism and 
ongoing evolution – recognizing that there are 
many opportunities for positive change – while 
also directing attention to those enduring aspects 
of Oceanside that lend the City its own identity. 
Oceanside is a distinctive and multifaceted com-
munity that displays a unique blend of coastal and 
inland characteristics. 
In many respects, Oceanside is akin to the other 
cities within the Highway 78 corridor – i.e., Vista, 
San Marcos, and Escondido. These cities have sim-
ilar socioeconomic profiles and housing markets, 
and they all have significant Hispanic populations. 
They share watersheds, topographic features, and 
micro-climates. They all border expansive wild-
land areas. Additionally, all four of these cities 
are served by NCTD’s Sprinter rail service. The 
two oldest incorporated cities in North County, 
Oceanside and Escondido are both important 
gateways into the San Diego region.
At the same time, Oceanside resembles the neigh-
boring North County Coastal cities of Carlsbad, 
Encinitas, and Solana Beach. Connected by 
Interstate 5 and the Pacific Coast Highway, these 
cities share a coastline that affords a wide range 
of recreational opportunities. They also share 
coastal lagoons that serve to delineate the cities 
and lend a unique visual character to the North 
Photo Credit: Samantha Jean; Cover Photo Credit: Mark Neal 


2-5
REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
County Coastal subregion. All of these cities are 
popular visitor destinations, particularly during 
the summer months. They all face serious beach 
erosion issues that require a coordinated regional 
response.
Oceanside’s most recognizable and character-de-
fining features include three miles of coastline on 
the Pacific Ocean, the Oceanside Municipal Pier, 
the Oceanside Small Craft Harbor, Mission San 
Luis Rey de Francia, the San Luis Rey River, the 
Rosicrucian Fellowship/Mount Ecclesia, Guajome 
Regional Park, El Corazon, and the South Morro 
Hills agricultural area. These venues draw visitors 
from around the world.  
The Municipal Pier —one of the longest on the 
West Coast—is an iconic coastal amenity and an 
essential aspect of the City’s brand. The north 
and south sides of the pier feature two consis-
tent, high-quality surf breaks in Oceanside, where 
many surf contests are held.
Founded in 1798 and known as the King of the 
Missions, Mission San Luis Rey de Francia is 
Oceanside’s most notable historic resource. The 
Mission is surrounded by the Mission San Luis Rey 
Historic Area, which is governed by design guide-
lines that seek to maintain and enhance the area’s 
historic character.  
Once the site of a sand and gravel mine, the 465-
acre El Corazon property is a premier regional rec-
reational venue, featuring a youth soccer complex, 
an aquatic center, a sports arena, a nature trail, 
and several public parks. Located in the geograph-
ic center of Oceanside, El Corazon is supported by 
several nearby hotels and dining establishments 
and can be accessed from the Rancho del Oro 
Sprinter Station. El Corazon is quickly becoming 
one of Oceanside’s most well-known destinations. 
Other notable destinations contributing to 
Oceanside’s character and brand include the 
City’s segment of the Pacific Coast Highway (aka 
Highway 101), the Oceanside Art Museum, the 
California Surf Museum, Heritage Park, Buena 
Vista Lagoon Nature Center, and Bob Maxwell 
Memorial Airfield.   
Oceanside’s character and culture are greatly 
influenced by the City’s location. Situated in the 
northwest corner of San Diego County and bound-
ed by the Pacific Ocean and expansive open space 
areas, the City affords sweeping views that extend 
to distant mountain ranges and stretches of coast-
line. The City’s hills, mesas, canyons, and riparian 
corridors serve to break up the built environment 
and provide visual relief. These natural features 
physically delineate and define Oceanside’s neigh-
borhoods and commercial districts. 


Photo Credit: Terry Brown
OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
2-6
Oceanside encompasses a diverse array of employ-
ment areas, commercial centers, and neighborhoods 
reflecting various eras of the City’s development, 
ranging from the Spanish colonial period to the 
present day. 
For decades, development was concentrated in the 
City’s coastal area. In the 1960s, the City began 
to sprawl into the San Luis Rey River Valley, the 
Oceanside Boulevard corridor, and the Highway 78 
corridor. Replacing natural open space and farmland, 
development in these inland areas of Oceanside is 
characterized by single-family subdivisions of vari-
able density, strip commercial centers, and busi-
ness/industrial parks. To accommodate develop-
ment in these areas, the San Luis Rey River, Loma 
Alta Creek, and Buena Vista Creek have been chan-
nelized. Residential development on inland hillsides 
and ridgelines has significantly modified natural 
landforms, and manufactured slopes are common. 
However, development in the City’s inland areas is 
intertwined with recreational open space, habitat 
conservation areas, riparian corridors, and undevel-
opable slopes, all of which afford expansive views 
and contribute to a sense of openness. 
Over the past 25 years, the City’s coastal area 
has undergone extensive redevelopment. The 
Downtown District has been transformed by tran-
sit-oriented development, high-quality resort hotels, 
and a variety of public improvements. Residential 
areas to the west of Coast Highway have seen 
single-family homes replaced by contemporary 
attached housing projects (both condominiums and 
rental apartments). Enabled by density bonus law 
and other state legislation, midrise mixed-use proj-
ects with income-restricted units are materializing 
along Coast Highway alongside commercial uses 
and cultural amenities.
Traversing through the eastern portion and con-
necting this to the west are three major corridors: 
Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and Vista 
Way/Highway 78. These three corridors, together 
with the Coast Highway, are key commercial centers 
for the City. Cohesive redevelopment of these cor-
ridors offers the possibility of not just accommodat-
ing the city’s future growth but re-shaping the city’s 
identity and improving neighborhood livability.
The northeastern corner of the City features South 
Morro Hills, an agricultural area with about 3,500 
acres of the last remnant land in the coastal San 
Diego region in active agricultural use. The dramat-
ic terrain and elevation gain in this part of the city 
provide expansive views extending to the ocean in 
many locations. General Plan policies seek to main-
tain the overall character of the area, while promot-
ing the introduction of agritourism uses to ensure 
continued viability of commercial agriculture. 


2-7
REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
PURPOSE AND INTENT
The Remarkable Community Element (RC) seeks 
to reinforce distinctive and positive attributes of 
the City, preserve historic and cultural resources, 
and enhance community identity and the sense of 
place. Policies address the shift to infill and rede-
velopment and shaping this new growth pattern 
to meet community goals relating to climate mit-
igation and adaptation, mobility, and economic 
development. 
A fundamental objective of the RC is to ensure 
that future growth and change contribute to 
Oceanside’s livability, economic prosperity, and 
visual quality. To this end, the RC outlines a broad 
framework for transforming the City’s commer-
cial corridors into walkable activity centers that 
provide new housing and employment opportuni-
ties. Additionally, in conjunction with the Efficient 
and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU), the 
RC provides guidance for establishing appropri-
ate linkages and buffers between different uses, 
open spaces, and transportation systems, ensur-
ing harmony between the City’s built and natural 
environments. 
Community Priorities
The Oceanside community prizes the City’s 
numerous scenic, cultural, and visual resourc-
es, and the City’s overall ambiance and sense 
of place. Community members broadly support 
infill and redevelopment within the City’s major 
commercial corridors, if changes result in more 
housing options, better access to essential goods 
and services, safer streets and public spaces, 
walkability, and improved visual quality. Focusing 
the City’s growth on the corridors provides the 
added benefit of maintaining the scale and char-
acter of existing neighborhoods. Many residents 
also expressed a desire for more frequent and 
safe connections for pedestrians and bicycles 
throughout the city, as well as increased access 
to commercial centers, parks, and lively public 
spaces. There is also support for maintaining the 
rural/agricultural character of South Morro Hills, 
albeit with diverse opinions on the best way to 
achieve this goal.  
Relationship to Specific, Community, 
and Other Plans
The Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific 
Plan, developed concurrently with the General 
Plan, outlines policies and design standards 
for the corridors in greater detail. An Active 
Transportation Plan—for supporting walking and 
biking—is also under development, synchronized 
with the General Plan. The General Plan also calls 
for preparation of a South Morro Hills Community 
Plan to outline strategies for agricultural conser-
vation and the promotion of agritourism. As per 
State law, all specific and community plans are 
required to be consistent with the General Plan.  
TOPIC AREAS
The RC element is not required under State law, but 
is included in the General Plan to celebrate, pre-
serve, and enhance characteristics that contribute 
to Oceanside’s sense of place and community liva-
bility, and to improve conditions that detract from 
quality of life, create or perpetuate inequities, 
inhibit economic development, and diminish com-
munity pride. Under state law, all General Plan ele-
ments, whether required or optional, carry equal 
weight, and must be consistent with one another 
in terms of policy direction. Topics addressed in 
the RC include community character and design, 
cultural and historic resources, Oceanside’s iden-
tity as a unique visitor destination, and the City’s 
seventeen Neighborhood Planning Areas.
The RC establishes goals, policies, and actions 
meant to support a visually appealing and safe 
urban form and to protect and enhance the places 
that make Oceanside unique. The element pres-
ents frameworks for each of the City’s neigh-
borhoods that seek to identify opportunities for 
improvement while still valuing and preserving 
the existing character of each neighborhood.


OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN

a diverse mix of uses. This area includes the City’s 
many coastal amenities and the Downtown District, 
both of which draw many visitors. 
The expansive inland area of the City is marked by 
hills and mesas that delineate three watercourses 
and associated riparian areas that extend to the 
Pacific Ocean. Each watercourse parallels a major 
east-west roadway and commercial corridor: the 
San Luis Rey River runs along the Mission Avenue/
Highway 76 corridor; Loma Alta Creek extends 
through the Oceanside Boulevard corridor; and 
Buena Vista Creek and Lagoon stretch along the 
Vista Way/Highway 78 corridor. Many of the City’s 
regional-serving commercial uses are located along 
Highway 78, while commercial uses within the 
Mission Avenue and Oceanside Boulevard corri-
dors tend to be more neighborhood and commu-
nity-serving. All three of these corridors feature 
somewhat outdated, auto-oriented commercial 
strip centers. The City’s three east-west corridors 
intersect three major north-south roadways—El 
Camino Real, Rancho Del Oro Drive, and College 
Boulevard—forming a street super-grid. Nodal areas 
within this grid include commercial centers, public 
parks, transit stations, and schools (e.g., Mira Costa 
Community College). Situated between these corri-
dors are residential neighborhoods, industrial uses 
and business centers, recreational open space, and 
natural habitat. 
Sloping terrain, limited cross-walks, fast-moving 
traffic, and gaps in sidewalk can make walking 
difficult along these major corridors. As outlined 
in the Integrated Mobility Element (IM), the City 
seeks to “complete” these corridors by improving 
active transportation facilities and transit service 
2.2 Community 
Character and Design
At the citywide scale, Oceanside’s location and 
geography play a key role in shaping the City’s 
overall form and structure. At a district or neigh-
borhood scale, key factors that affect community 
design are the overall pattern and size of blocks 
and the frequency of through streets, as well as 
the overall dispersion and intensity of uses. These 
factors in turn affect the accessibility and walk-
ability of the City – for example, more frequent 
connections can enable easier navigation between 
places, whereas less frequent connections may 
require circuitous travel (even between physi-
cally close locations). The design and the quality 
of the public realm also play a key role in shap-
ing the everyday living and working experience. 
This includes the design of streets and sidewalks, 
parks and plazas, tree canopy and shade, the rela-
tionship of buildings to streets and sidewalks, and 
building design and appearance. 
The goals and policies for community character 
and design address overall community character 
and design at different scales – from city form 
and block size to how people navigate the city and 
utilize and experience the public realm. The goals 
and policies presented in this section emphasize 
connectivity, clarity, comfort, and creativity in the 
design of buildings and the public realm.
WHAT IS THE PUBLIC REALM?
The term ‘public realm’ refers to all parts of 
the built environment where the public has 
free and unrestricted access. 
URBAN FORM
Oceanside’s residential neighborhoods and com-
mercial districts reflect the eras in which they were 
developed. To the west of Interstate 5, an approx-
imately half-mile-wide and three-mile-long stretch 
paralleling the Pacific Ocean comprises the Townsite 
and South Oceanside Neighborhood Planning 
Areas. This area features a traditional develop-
ment pattern, with short blocks and alleyways and 
Photo Credit: Spurlock Landscape Architects


2-9
REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
and facilitating pedestrian-oriented development. 
Additionally, the City seeks to introduce and 
expand pedestrian and bicycle trails along the east-
west riparian corridors and link these trails to key 
destinations. 
To limit urban sprawl, conserve open space and 
farmland, and protect the character and tranquility 
of existing single-family neighborhoods, the City 
has designed a policy and regulatory framework 
meant to channel future housing and employment 
growth into the Oceanside’s major commercial cor-
ridors. Infill and redevelopment within these corri-
dors will facilitate public realm improvements that 
make walking and biking safer and more comfort-
able. Frequent pedestrian connections, and, where 
possible, small block sizes, can help foster pedes-
trian activity. New development that relates to the 
street through prominent entrances and windows 
can provide a sense of safety and security while 
creating a more interactive and visually appealing 
environment for pedestrians. Articulated facades 
and rooflines, setbacks, and landscaping can pro-
vide for light and air while also creating a welcoming 
“outdoor room” ambience within the public realm 
that promotes walking, shopping, and gathering. 
This section of the RC outlines goals and polices 
that promote placemaking through people-oriented 
urban design. These goals and policies are meant to 
promote fundamental placemaking principles while 
also allowing for creative and context-sensitive 
approaches to both private development and public 
realm improvements.  
SENSE OF PLACE
“Sense of place” commonly refers to how an area 
is perceived by residents and visitors, and, in turn, 
this perception largely determines how residents 
and visitors navigate and interact with the area. 
A strong sense of place not only renders an area 
readily identifiable but also inspires feelings of 
attachment and pride. Areas with a strong sense 
of place tend to hold more meaning and value for 
both residents and visitors. Conversely, people 
tend to feel less invested in areas that lack a 
strong sense of place.   
A fundamental goal of the RC is to facilitate pri-
vate development and public improvements that 
imbue a strong sense of place to not only provide 
Oceanside with a distinct and positive identity, but 
also to neighborhood identity. Fostering a strong 
sense of place throughout Oceanside can better 
connect residents and visitors to their surround-
ings, promote civic identity and engagement, and 
foster community pride.  
Areas that provide a strong sense of place tend 
to be unified around conspicuous and compatible 
visual themes, which are evoked by architectural 
details, finish materials, color schemes, lighting, 
signage, paving, landscaping, and other interven-
tions. Settings that convey a strong sense of place 
also tend to have distinct boundaries and defined 
points of entry, which not only distinguish them 
from other areas but also serve to orient and 
guide those who move through them.   
“A distinctive and legible environment not 
only offers security but also heightens the 
potential depth and intensity of human 
experience.”
- Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City
“The more successfully a city mingles every-
day diversity of uses and users in its every-
day streets, the more successfully its people 
enliven and support [its public spaces].”
- Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of

REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
A strong sense of place is often reinforced by 
interactive 
elements, 
including 
storefronts 
that allow for window shopping, public art that 
engages the intellect and the imagination, street 
furnishings that allow for observation and con-
versation, playgrounds that encourage physical 
activity, kiosks that provide information such as 
weather forecasts, transit schedules, and calen-
dars of upcoming events, and music that compels 
us to tap our feet, clap our hands, and dance. 
Additionally, settings that embrace and draw 
attention to their history also tend to create a 
strong sense of place.  
A strong sense of place provides residents and 
visitors with enriching experiences, interesting 
stories, and a sense of belonging. Residents and 
business owners in areas that exude a strong 
sense of place are typically more engaged in pro-
tecting and enhancing these areas, while visitors 
are more motivated to linger in such settings, 
return to them, and share their experience of 
them with others. These realities have important 
implications for public health and safety, commu-
nity building, and economic development.
SIGNAGE 
Signage of various types often has a prominent 
presence in the built environment, particularly in 
commercial districts and along major roadways. 
Essential for public safety, wayfinding, marketing, 
and public information, signage is protected by the 
1st Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which 
classifies signage as a form of protected speech 
and limits the ability of local governments to reg-
ulate sign content. However, local governments 
can establish policies and standards that promote 
tasteful, high-quality signage that furthers their 
urban design goals. 
Through the thoughtful regulation of the various 
aspects of signage – i.e., amount, size, placement, 
and type – communities can create a safer, more 
navigable, and more attractive public realm. When 
not properly regulated, signage can be distracting, 
disorienting, and unsightly. Signage that impedes 
adequate sight distance can create undo risk for 
pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists. Signage that 
obscures and/or conflicts with building architec-
ture and landscaping can diminish curb appeal and 
the surrounding streetscape. Signage exhibiting 
The farmers market helps build a sense of place in Downtown Oceanside.


OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
2-12
uninspired design and low-quality materials can 
not only create a sterile and unappealing environ-
ment but also reflect poorly on the businesses the 
signage seeks to promote. Moreover, such signage 
can be more susceptible to vandalism, as it tends 
to convey a lack of care and attention. Conversely, 
well-designed and well-maintained signage can 
contribute to the safety, comfort, visual quality 
and positive branding of a community. Indeed, 
providing first-rate, context-sensitive signage is 
one of the best ways in which businesses, resi-
dential developments, public uses, and the City 
itself can add charm and vibrancy to the public 
realm and, in turn, foster community identity and 
pride. The Remarkable Community Element there-
fore encourages the City to take a conscientious 
approach to the regulation of signage, recognizing 
that the overall quality of signage in Oceanside is a 
reflection of community character. 
The City’s signage regulations for non-residential 
uses have historically been very accommodating, 
allowing a significant amount of total sign area 
and placing few limitations on design, lighting, and 
materials. As a result, some stretches of the City’s 
commercial corridors are dominated by banal and 
oversized signage that detracts from a sense of 
place. Plastic-faced, internally-illuminated cabinet 
signs are common. Pole and pylon signs often dis-
play an abundance of text in different fonts and 
colors. Sign materials and textures often differ 
from base materials and textures (e.g., plastic 
signs attached to stone or brick structures). While 
the City requires comprehensive sign programs 
for large commercial centers, to ensure some 
level of quality and consistency, these programs 
aren’t always adhered to when signs are subse-
quently added or replaced. The City can promote 
improvements over time through updated stan-
dards, diligent review of sign permit applications, 
and amortization of non-conforming signs. 
While there are different opinions about what consti-
tutes tasteful, high-quality signage, communities with 
a strong commitment to urban design tend to privi-
lege signs that exhibit the following characteristics:    
• Natural materials, rather than plastic and other 
composites 
 
— Metal 
 
— Stone 
 
— Wood 
 
— Porcelain and other ceramics 
 
— Acrylic and foam, when designed to mimic nat-
ural materials 
• Dimensional letters and logos, rather than flat panels 
 
— Channel letters 
 
— Pinned letters 
 
— Routed metal and wood 
 
— Cast metal 
• Painted signs 
• Indirect or halo lighting, rather than translucent 
face-lit cabinets or channel letters 
• Monument signs, rather than pole or pylon signs 
The signage types outlined above not only tend to be 
more aesthetically pleasing but also more environmen-
tally friendly and energy efficient than other signage 
types. In general, signage materials should be renew-
able and/or recyclable and lighting should utilize LED, 
compact fluorescent, and/or other technologies that 
achieve high per-watt luminosity. 
With respect to the amount, size, and type of sig-
nage allowed, the City should generally limit the total 
number and maximum dimension of signs to what is 
necessary to achieve adequate visibility. Signage should 
be proportional to the site area and the scale of devel-
opment. Pole and pylon signs should be limited to high-
way-oriented sites that would otherwise not be visible 
to potential customers. 
In terms of the placement of signs, by and large, com-
mercial signage should not be visible from or direct 
glare toward residential areas. On larger sites, sign clut-
ter should be avoided through a balance of wall signs 
and free-standing signs. Signs should be reserved for 
the most conspicuous building frontages.  
Illuminated signage should not contribute to ambient 
light or create light pollution. 
These guidelines are meant to provide for creativity 
and a diversity of styles that foster a visual environment 
that is at once rich, intelligible, and organized. The City 
is encouraged to work with applicants to ensure that 
proposed signage achieves its fundamental purpose of 
drawing attention and providing information without 
overwhelming or compromising the visual quality of its 
surroundings.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN

ACCESSIBILITY IN THE PUBLIC 
REALM
To create a truly equitable and enjoyable city, the 
public realm should be accessible to all community 
members, including children, elderly people, dis-
abled people, and those of limited means. People 
of all backgrounds should feel welcome in these 
areas. Oceanside’s diversity should be on display 
in the public realm – not only through the people 
who occupy it, but also through the physical fea-
tures that contribute to its ambience – architec-
ture, public art, signage, etc.  
Establishing and maintaining a welcoming public 
realm often involves the removal of both physi-
cal and psychological barriers to access and use. 
Such barriers include a disconnected street net-
work, high-speed vehicle traffic, a lack of active 
transportation infrastructure, a lack of greenery 
and tree canopy, buildings that do not engage 
the street, poor signage, poor lighting, and a lack 
of refuge for pedestrians (e.g., shade structures, 
outdoor furnishings). Sidewalks with uneven sur-
faces, a lack of curb ramps, and obstacles that 
require a lot of redirection can be difficult and 
stressful to navigate for all users, not just elderly 
and disabled people. While well-designed streets, 
sidewalks, and pedestrian connections are essen-
tial throughout the City, they are even more crit-
ical around high activity areas, such as schools, 
parks, and neighborhood commercial centers. The 
physical safety of all street users is addressed in 
full in the Integrated Mobility (IM) element.
“We have an obligation to ensure that public 
spaces are accessible, inclusive, and at the 
service of all community members who want 
to come together.” 
- Lisa Cholmondeley and Hao Ko, Designing 
Cities that Are Open and Equitable
SENSE OF SAFETY IN THE PUBLIC 
REALM
Everyone should feel safe and secure in public 
spaces. However, throughout the community 
engagement process in support of the General 
Plan Update, a significant percentage of residents 
stated that they often feel uncomfortable in public 
spaces in Oceanside, especially those that are 
unkempt or lack “eyes on the street.” This concern 
is particularly prevalent in the youth community. 
While many of Oceanside’s young people would 
like to spend more time in public spaces, they are 
wary of who they may encounter in dormant and 
un-surveilled areas. Finding ways to activate such 
areas is essential to creating a sense of safety and 
security.   
Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design 
(CPTED) is a crime prevention philosophy based 
on the theory that the proper design and effective 
use of the built environment, can lead to a reduc-
tion in the fear of crime as well as an improvement 
in the quality of life. CPTED works by decreasing 
a criminal’s ability to commit a crime and increas-
ing the chances that the crime will be seen and 
reported. CPTED goes beyond traditional security 
methods by naturally integrating security mea-
sures into the community. The goal of all CPTED 
applications is to increase the quality of life, 
decrease the fear of crime, and decrease crime. 
Because different people or groups may have 
varying perceptions of what makes a community 
feel safe, CPTED guidelines need to be tailored to 
response to a community’s context, diversity, and 
unique safety issues. CPTED principles should 
also be coupled with acknowledgment of racial 
profiling that results in disproportionate harm and 
violence to Black, Indigenous, Latinx, and Asian 
communities. 
Examples of CPTED interventions typically ref-
erence lighting, line of sight, and other visibility 
issues, clearly defined spaces, and access. For 
example, building exteriors, parking lots, and 
parking garages should be well lit. Property lines 
and private areas should be defined with plant-
ings, pavement treatments, short walls, or fences. 
Further, landscaping should be maintained and 
trimmed to avoid creating blind spots or hiding 
spots. The City of Oceanside will continue to 
apply these CPTED principles in the design of 
Photo Credit: Spurlock Landscape Architects

new development in order to enhance public 
safety and reduce calls for service and will explore 
opportunities to more intentionally integrate con-
text-specific recommendations in partnership 
with community.
VISUAL RESOURCES AND URBAN 
FORESTRY
Visual Resources
Oceanside’s coastline, natural landforms, ripar-
ian areas, parks, urban landscape, and vistas of 
nearby mountain ranges and the ocean contrib-
ute significantly to the city’s visual quality, as do 
the city’s well-kept residential neighborhoods, 
historic resources, and iconic buildings. However, 
the City’s aesthetic character is diminished by 
non-descript and poorly-maintained develop-
ment, disorganized land use patterns, inconsistent 
design themes, an abundance of surface parking 
abutting the street frontage, and a lack of tree 
canopy and plantable surface area. Moreover, the 
key gateways into the City—e.g. along Interstate 5 
and State Routes 76 and 78—are visually incoher-
ent. There are few markers that announce entry 
into the City, and those that exist generally lack 
visual interest and a consistent theme.
The City can enhance visual quality through 
greater attention to fundamental urban design 
principles, including pedestrian orientation, con-
nectivity, transparency, legibility, indoor-outdoor 
space, urban greening, and a synergetic mix of 
uses. The City can also foster a greater sense of 
neighborhood identity, encourage better stew-
ardship of both public and private space, estab-
lish form-based design standards, preserve and 
enhance scenic views, and integrate aesthetic 
upgrades into capital improvement projects.
Urban Forestry
The benefits of urban trees are vast and well-es-
tablished. Trees cool the streets and surrounding 
areas, help conserve energy, improve air quality, 
absorb and sequester carbon dioxide from the 
atmosphere, capture rainwater, prevent erosion, 
protect the quality of surface waters, provide habi-
tat, make the public realm more pleasant, enhance 
a sense of place, reduce stress, beautify streets-
capes and spaces, and provide economic benefits

REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
A healthy urban forest, comprised of public and 
privately maintained trees throughout the com-
munity, is an integral component of a sustainable 
and equitable city. Yet trees in cities face a vari-
ety of threats, including increasing summer heat 
and frequent droughts, pests, storm events, chal-
lenges in funding maintenance costs, and some 
conflicts with underground and overhead utilities 
and development activity. Policies in this chap-
ter aim to sustain and enhance the city’s urban 
forest, a valuable environmental resource and an 
important component of a pleasant public realm 
experience.
Parkways
Many areas of the City feature parkways – i.e., 
spaces between the curb and sidewalk meant 
to accommodate landscape.  Adjacent property 
owners are responsible for maintaining parkways 
along their street frontage.  
When properly maintained, parkways provide a 
wide range of community benefits:
• Separating vehicle travel lanes and curbside 
parking from sidewalk, thereby enhancing 
pedestrian safety and comfort and contributing 
to walkability; 
• Supporting the urban forest, which provides 
shade, passive cooling, carbon sequestration, 
stormwater capture, and refuge for birds and 
other wildlife; 
• Maintaining a sense of openness and softening 
the appearance of the built environment; and
• Enhancing public health and wellness, as 
demonstrated by studies showing that spending 
time around trees and other plant life reduces 
stress, lowers blood pressure, and improves 
mood; and
• Increasing property values.
The City will amend its parkway ordinance to 
emphasize that parkways should be maintained as 
permeable and plantable area, with limited imper-
vious hardscape.
LIGHT POLLUTION
Visual characteristics and the effects of lighting and 
glare can have a disruptive impact on the environ-
ment and the quality of life in surrounding neigh-
borhoods. This effect is often referred to as light 
LIGHT POLLUTION COMPONENTS
Light pollution is excessive and inappropri-
ate artificial light. The four components of 
light pollution are often combined and may 
overlap:
• Urban Sky Glow: The brightening of the 
night sky over inhabited areas.
• Light Trespass: Light falling where it is not 
intended, wanted, or needed.
• Glare: Excessive brightness which causes 
visual discomfort. High levels of glare can 
decrease visibility.
• Clutter: Bright, confusing, and excessive 
groupings of light sources, commonly 
found in over-lit urban areas. The prolif-
eration of clutter contributes to urban sky 
glow, trespass, and glare.
National Optical Astronomy Observatory 
(NOAO)Dark Skies Awareness. http://www.
darkskiesawareness.org/
Light pollution downtown.
pollution, which is defined as the excessive and 
inappropriate use of artificial light and is common 
in urban environments. Light pollution can nega-
tively affect residents during the night by producing 
unwanted glare, which can affect sleep patterns and 
health. Light pollution also affects wildlife by dis-
rupting nocturnal activities, such as sleeping, hunt-
ing, mating, and migratory behavior, and can con-
fuse wildlife.1 In addition to protecting viewsheds 
that are important to the City, zoning ordinances 
regulate lighting in order to protect the visual com-
fort of residents and minimize the negative impacts 
to wildlife. Given the intermixed urban and natural 
areas that characterize Oceanside’s settings, reduc-
ing light pollution can have a healthier effect for res-
idents and wildlife alike.

Dark Skies Awareness. Accessed via web 6/2021. http://

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
2-18
GOALS AND POLICIES
GOALS 
2-A 
Oceanside’s built environment will be 
easy to navigate, visually appealing, and 
accommodating of social engagement, 
community building, physical activity, 
and cultural enrichment.
2-B 
Public spaces will be designed to wel-
come and safely accommodate all com-
munity members, including pedestrians, 
bicyclists, children, the elderly, and the 
disabled.
2-C 
The City’s built environment will convey 
a strong sense of place through the 
presence and thoughtful arrangement of 
essential and character-defining public 
realm improvements, fostering a sense of 
community and civic pride.
2-D 
The City’s natural environment and urban 
tree canopy will equitably enhance the 
city’s visual quality, mitigate the urban 
heat island effect, and improve the expe-
rience of the public realm. 
2-E 
Entry into Oceanside will be conspic-
uously and attractively announced at 
gateway locations and the City will work 
with neighboring jurisdictions to ensure 
that transitional areas within the built 
environment are consistently maintained 
and demarcated. 
2-F 
New development will contribute to the 
functionality, coherence, accessibility, 
visual quality, and unique character of the 
City’s built environment. 
POLICIES
Building Design
2-1 
All buildings should be sited and designed 
to engage the sidewalk and the public 
realm. While the design context and solu-
tions will vary across the city, in general 
this means ensuring that buildings are 
oriented to the street, promote pedes-
trian safety and “eyes on the street” with 
parking tucked away behind buildings, and 
provide linkages to pedestrian paths and 
direct access to transit where present. 
2-2 
Minimize the footprint of parking through 
innovative design, shared parking facilities, 
and transportation demand management 
strategies.
2-3 
Buildings on a corner should treat both 
street sides as “fronts,” adhere to the 
minimum and any maximum front setback 
requirements along both streets and 
include pedestrian-friendly building design 
features such as windows, doors, walk-
ways, and signage along both streets. 
2-4 
Street-facing 
elevations 
shall 
include 
conspicuous entrances that provide plane 
breaks and visual interest. 
2-5 
New development should exhibit “five-
sided architecture” that provides visual 
interest on all building elevations and 
visible roof areas.  
2-6 
Long wall planes shall be accented with 
fenestration and decorative elements 
– e.g., tile, grillwork, metal cladding, mold-
ings, color bands. 
2-7 
Vertical landscape elements shall be 
employed to soften the appearance of 
large buildings.  
2-8 
Trash enclosure walls and gates must 
be architecturally compatible with the 
building design and should be carefully 
integrated into the site plan. 
Photo Credit: Spurlock Landscape Architects


2-19
REMARKABLE COMMUNITY 2
Mixed Use Buildings
2-9 
Mixed use buildings should be responsive 
to adjacent neighborhoods and minimize 
impacts including from noise, reduced pri-
vacy, and shadows by stepping buildings 
back, placing windows to minimize privacy 
impacts, and siting noise generating uses 
away from existing residential or other 
sensitive uses. 
Retail and Commercial Buildings
2-10 
Large retail establishments on large lots 
(e.g., full-service grocery stores, home 
improvement stores, department stores) 
should utilize vertical space, incorporate 
ample fenestration, activate street front-
ages with outdoor merchandising and 
ancillary uses, and provide pedestrian 
access through the site via arcades and 
pathways.   
2-11 
In commercial districts, encourage more 
intense and higher-profile development at 
major street intersections.  
2-12 
Require conspicuous primary entrances 
that are either recessed or accented with 
canopies or other architectural elements.
2-13 
Require that buildings located at street 
corners include corner entrances, mitered 
windows, and/or other architectural ele-
ments that avoid or soften sharp angles 
at the ground level and enhance sight 
distance for pedestrians.
2-14 
To the extent feasible, screen parking from 
the street frontage. Appropriate screening 
methods include landscaping, berms, grill-
work, decorative fencing, etc.
2-15 
Promote shared parking facilities that pro-
vide a “park once” experience for patrons.
2-16 
Encourage retail façade design that both 
supports window display and discourages 
the storage of merchandise in areas visible 
from public spaces.
2-17 
Ensure that buildings are designed to allow 
for the architectural integration of signage.
Industrial Buildings
2-18 
Minimum front yard setbacks in industrial 
districts should be determined by site 
design elements. Industrial projects that 
locate parking away from the street front-
age, exceed minimum landscaping and tree 
canopy requirements, and incorporate 
enhanced pedestrian amenities should 
benefit from reduced front yard setbacks.  
2-19 
Industrial buildings shall be composed of 
sturdy materials that convey permanence 
– e.g., precast concrete, masonry, stone, 
brick.  
2-20 
Industrial projects should maximize vertical 
space. Multistory industrial development 
is encouraged.   
2-21 
Industrial buildings shall be designed to 
accommodate all industrial processes 
within enclosed and adequately insulated 
spaces.   
2-22 
Outdoor storage shall be limited and 
allowed only when fully screened from 
public spaces. 
2-23 
Loading and service areas shall be substan-
tially screened from public spaces. 
2-24 
Industrial projects shall provide conspicuous 
paths of travel for pedestrians and utilize 
enhanced paving to distinguish pedestrian 
paths within vehicle circulation areas. 
2-25 
Industrial projects should consider the 
integration of public art, consistent with the 
visual character of the surrounding area.

Accessibility in the Public Realm
2-26 
Pursue roadway design that balances 
efficient vehicle through-put with traffic 
calming that contributes to pedestrian 
and bicycle safety and reduces noise and 
air pollution. Potential design elements 
include 
minimum-width 
traffic 
lanes, 
roundabout intersections, curb bulb-outs, 
chicanes and other path deviation devices, 
and variable paving treatments.
2-27 
Incorporate streetscape design elements 
(e.g., paving accents, landscaping, curvilin-
ear sidewalks) that help to visually break up 
long, uninterrupted stretches of roadway.  
2-28 
Where feasible, design pedestrian facilities 
in Pedestrian Priority Zones (see Figure 
2-1) to accommodate an edge zone, a 
landscape and furnishing zone, a through-
way zone, and a buffer zone between the 
throughway zone and buildings. See the 
SSCSP for more detail on the Pedestrian 
Priority Zones.
2-29 
Require new development to provide fre-
quent pedestrian connections to adjacent 
neighborhoods and local amenities includ-
ing commercial areas, parks, recreation 
centers, trails, and transit stations.
2-30 
Ensure that new pedestrian facilities are 
ADA-compliant and that disabled persons 
have equal access to their homes, places of 
work, shopping venues, and transit service 
from the public right-of-way.  
2-31 
Explore the viability of public restrooms in 
high-traffic commercial districts.
2-32 
Expand and improve pedestrian and bicy-
cle trails throughout the city and create 
linkages between the SLR River Trail, 
Coastal Trail, and Inland Rail Trail.
Sense of Safety in the Public Realm
2-33 
Consider ways to proactively address 
blighted conditions on private property, 
while encouraging community members to 
report such conditions to the City. 
2-34 
Work with the business community to 
enhance maintenance of public spaces 
in commercial districts. Explore funding 
mechanisms to address maintenance costs.
2-35 
Require and actively enforce timely repair 
of broken windows and other conspicuous 
damage to the exterior of buildings and 
ancillary structures. 
2-36 
Promote building design that provides for 
natural surveillance of the public realm.
2-37 
Encourage businesses to establish an 
active presence on alley frontages with 
building transparency, outdoor merchan-
dising and dining areas, bicycle parking, 
etc. Where these elements are in proxim-
ity to residential neighborhoods, require 
design features (e.g., fencing, screening 
landscape) that minimize noise, glare, and 
other emissions. 
2-38 
Enhance the appearance of alleys through 
landscaping, decorative lighting, open 
and/or low-profile fencing, and screening 
of waste receptacles, utilities, and other 
elements that detract from visual quality.
2-39 
In isolated areas, install and announce the 
presence of security cameras.
2-40 
Apply the principles of Crime Prevention 
through Environmental Design (CPTED) in 
the design of public realm improvements 
and ensure adequate lighting, natural 
surveillance, clear distinctions between 
public and private space, and the use of 
resilient materials that reduce maintenance 
requirements.  
2-41 
Continue to apply CPTED principles in the 
design of new development and encour-
age the provision of adequate public 
lighting, windows overlooking streets or 
parking lots, and paths to increase pedes-
trian activity within private development 
projects and public facilities in order to 
enhance public safety and reduce calls for 
service.
2-42 
Coordinate with the North County Transit 
District and other transportation agencies 
to enhance the safety and security of 
transit facilities.
