VITAL AND SUSTAINABLE RESOURCES 5
5.7 Agricultural 
Resources
Agricultural resources in Oceanside are concen-
trated in South Morro Hills, located in the northeast 
corner of the City. South Morro Hills encompasses 
a 5.4-square mile (3,500 acre) area of agricultural 
land that supports both commercial and avocational 
farming operations as well as estate residential use. 
Figure 5-8 shows areas designated for agricultural 
use under this General Plan. Over three-quar-
ters of the land in South Morro Hills is classified 
as one of the following types of farmland: Prime 
Farmland, Farmland of Statewide Importance, or 
Unique Farmland, as designated by the California 
Department of Conservation (see Figure 5-9). A 
smaller swath of farmland is located immediately 
south of South Morro Hills, along the southern 
banks of the San Luis Rey River. Prevalent crops 
within South Morro Hills include avocados, toma-
toes, berries, cannabis, and a wide variety of orna-
mentals. Wine grapes and coffee have recently 
been introduced to the area. In recent years, farm-
ers have been experimenting with new, higher-value 
crops, including coffee, cherimoya, and other exotic 
fruits and vegetables.  
The South Morro Hills area is under a large number 
of different ownerships, with parcel sizes ranging 
from less than three acres to several larger than 160 
acres. While the area’s existing Agricultural land use 
and zoning designations are ostensibly intended to 
support farming, applicable zoning standards allow 
for 2.5-acre residential subdivision. As of 2023, 
there were approximately 150 single-family homes 
in South Morro Hills. Through the City’s planned 
unit development provisions (which do not require 
that agricultural uses be maintained), higher den-
sities can be achieved, as evidenced by the North 
River Farms project approved in 2020. This project 
is projected to add nearly 400 new housing units 
to South Morro Hills. North River Farms will be the 
first development in South Morro Hills to be served 
by sanitary sewer. All other housing in South Morro 
Hills is served by septic systems, as no sewer ser-
vice currently extends north of North River Road. 
FINANCIAL PRESSURES ON 
AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION
An evaluation conducted in early 2022 com-
pared supportable land values for single-family 
residential development in the South Morro 
Hills (SMH) community to comparable land 
sales of agricultural land in San Diego County. 
The survey of comparable land sales for agri-
cultural land demonstrated a median value of 
approximately $57,000 per gross acre, a figure 
that has been declining over the past five years. 
By comparison, a financial feasibility analysis of 
large-lot single-family residential development 
in the SMH community under existing zoning 
regulations concluded a supportable land value 
of $134,000 per gross acre. In effect, this com-
parison of agricultural versus residential land 
values demonstrates that SMH property owners 
are incentivized to sell or develop their property 
for residential use. Additionally, demand for 
housing has continued to grow throughout the 
County, as development of new housing supply 
has not kept pace with demand. Under current 
zoning, properties in SMH have more than two 
times as much value for residential use rather 
than agricultural use, providing great incentive 
to property owners to convert their land from 
agricultural to residential use.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
5-48
DEVELOPMENT PRESSURES ON 
FARMLAND
The City’s agricultural lands face significant develop-
ment pressure, as evidenced by the North River Farms 
housing development, approved by the City in 2020. 
The City’s agricultural zoning district provides for 2.5-
acre residential subdivision as well as “planned devel-
opment plans” that allow property owners and devel-
opers to propose custom land use and development 
standards. These mechanisms could result in wide-
spread conversion of farmland. While further study 
is needed to identify a solution to the development 
pressures on farmland, agritourism in South Morro 
Hills represents one alternative revenue source for 
local farmers that can help maintain existing farmland.
Along North River Road, Rainbow Municipal Water 
District conveys wastewater from Rainbow Municipal 
Water District to the San Luis Rey Water Reclamation 
Facility (SLRWRF). At present, no other sewer infra-
structure exists within San Morro Hills. The area is 
served by the City’s potable water system, has very 
limited stormwater conveyance infrastructure, and 
is not yet served by the Oceanside Recycled Water 
program. Any extension would need to be paid for by 
property owners. More intensive uses in the area, such 
as agritourism facilities, may require wastewater exten-
sion, as is the case with North River Farms.
AGRICULTURAL CONSERVATION
The only way to fully guarantee that active farming 
continues in South Morro Hills is for farmlands to be 
acquired by public agencies or land trusts, or  through 
the establishment of conservation easements. Any 
City acquisition will require substantial financial out-
lays, likely necessitating special Citywide tax measures, 
which is likely infeasible. Short of this, public policy can 
be directed to ensuring that farming remains economi-
cally viable and productive, providing other supportive 
measures, and seeking grants and other available fund-
ing for conservation. 
The General Plan presents several strategies for 
strengthening Oceanside’s active agricultural areas. 
Supportive Uses 
One avenue that the City has explored is increasing 
allowances for agritourism uses on agricultural land to 
provide an additional option for revenue. In 2017, the 
City amended the Zoning Code to allow lower-intensity 
(“Tier 1”) agritourism uses such as U-Pick operations, 
petting zoos, and farm stands. One obstacle to the 
development of agritourism and other supportive uses 
that would increase the financial viability of produc-
tion farming is the lack of access to City infrastructure 
systems, financing of which would require more devel-
opment than that would result from large-lot zoning or 
Tier 1 uses. While the City is not currently proposing 
expansion of infrastructure to the South Morro Hills 
neighborhood, doing so would open up the possibility 
for the allowance of additional (“Tier 2”) agritourism 
uses such as wedding venues, event spaces, and small 
inns. 
Grants
Other agriculture preservation mechanisms exist and 
should be further explored for applicability in South 
Morro Hills. One such program, the Sustainable 
Agricultural Lands Conservation Program (SALC), 
utilizes statewide Cap-and-Trade proceeds to pro-
tect agricultural lands that are at risk of conversion 
to other uses. Protecting farmland avoids increased 
emissions associated with development and provides 
an opportunity to capture carbon in the land base. 
SALC’s mission is to support California’s need for agri-
cultural conservation, economic growth, and sustain-
able development. SALC funds projects that protect 
at-risk agricultural lands from conversion to more pol-
lution-heavy land uses such as urban or rural residen-
tial development. The program provides two types of 
awards, Planning grants and Agricultural Conservation 
Acquisition grants. 
• Planning grants provide funds to develop plans 
for the protection of agricultural land at risk of 
conversion to non-agricultural uses. These plans 
support agricultural land conservation by protecting 
the land base and developing regional food systems. 
Plans may also recognize and protect environmental 
co-benefits of conserving agricultural lands. 


5-49
VITAL AND SUSTAINABLE RESOURCES 5
• Agricultural Conservation Acquisition grants are 
used to permanently protect agricultural lands 
that support infill and compact development. 
Agricultural Conservation Acquisition grants will 
be provided to purchase conservation easements 
or fee title to agricultural land. Acquisition grants 
are deed restrictions that landowners voluntarily 
place on their property to preserve the land’s 
agricultural uses. 
LOOKING AHEAD
Looking ahead, it is crucial to implement strategies 
that preserve and provide economic incentives for 
farming, preserve biological habitats, and estab-
lish an integrated network of open spaces. While 
expanding supportive uses such as agritourism can 
help maintain the economic feasibility of farming 
in Oceanside, it is important to address the lack 
of access to City infrastructure systems in South 
Morro Hills. More intensive agritourism uses could 
be leveraged in the future to finance the expansion 
of the appropriate infrastructure systems.
In addition to maintaining active agricultural uses 
in South Morro Hills, preserving biological habi-
tats is essential for maintaining the biodiversity 
and beauty of the region. Wetlands, riparian areas, 
grasslands, and areas of coastal sage scrub must 
be conserved, and wildlife movement networks 
along riparian corridors should be established or 
strengthened.
The establishment of an integrated network of open 
spaces is crucial to wildlife movement and biodiver-
sity, and to the overall sustainability and livability of 
the area. Creating a well-planned network of trails 
and open spaces will contribute to the protection 
of natural resources, enhanced wildlife habitat con-
nectivity, and an improved quality of life for resi-
dents and visitors.
While South Morro Hills is valued by many commu-
nity members for its bucolic ambience, the sense of 
openness it lends to inland portions of Oceanside, 
and the potential it holds for local food sourcing, 
agritourism, and agricultural research, the decision 
to continue farming operations in this corner of 
Oceanside rests with property owners. It is there-
fore essential that the City work with these prop-
erty owners to sustain and enhance the viability of 
farming as an economic enterprise.  
SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURAL 
PRACTICES
South Morro Hills is served by the City’s pota-
ble water system, has very limited stormwater 
conveyance infrastructure, and is not yet served 
by the Oceanside Recycled Water program. The 
expansion of the City’s recycled water network 
will help supplement water demands in SMH, as 
well as reduce reliance on groundwater for agri-
cultural use. 
South Morro Hills is home to several rich veg-
etation communities, particularly wetland and 
riparian areas along the San Luis Rey River and 
its tributaries. Sensitive habitats and species 
continue to be supported along wetlands and 
riparian corridors, as well as in limited areas of 
grasslands and sage scrub. Local endangered 
species, including Least Bell’s vireo, the south-
western willow flycatcher, the tricolored black-
bird, Stephan’s kangaroo rat, and the arroyo toad, 
may be present in the agricultural areas of South 
Morro Hills. It is imperative that these habitats 
be conserved, and wildlife movement networks 
along riparian corridors maintained and/or re-es-
tablished as opportunities arise.   
Agricultural cultivation has the potential to cause 
harmful health effects to surrounding communi-
ties through runoff and airborne dust and con-
taminants. For example, the areas near South 
Morro Hills have top 25th percentile statewide 
rankings for pesticide exposure. Working with 
farmers to transition to regenerative farming 
practices and phasing out pesticides and harmful 
agricultural byproducts will both improve the 
quality and sustainability of agricultural prod-
ucts, and reduce negative health and ecosystem 
impacts to the surrounding area. Please see the 
Healthy and Livable Communities Element for 
more information about health impacts near 
agricultural lands.

5.8 Mineral Resources
The City of Oceanside does not currently accom-
modate any mining operations. The Silica Sand 
Mining Company conducted sand and gravel 
mining on the El Corazon property until 1994, 
when the property was turned over to the City. 
Lawrence Canyon was also the site of sand and 
gravel mining in the 1950s.  While there are no 
known major mineral deposits within the City, 
the following goals and policies seek to ensure 
that any future mining operations are conducted 
in a safe, economically sustainable, and environ-
mental just manner.
GOALS AND POLICIES
GOALS
5-Q 
All mining operations in the City will be 
in compliance with the Surface Mining 
Reclamation Act, and will balance 
economic benefits, public safety and 
environmental equality.
POLICIES
Mining Operations
5-93 
If previously unknown major mineral 
deposits are found, create a process to 
balance the potential economic benefits 
with public safety, equity, and environ-
mental sustainability.
5-94 
Require that any lease agreements for 
any future mining operations within the 
City are written to prevent wastelands 
or other environmental byproducts of 
mining.
5-95 
Do not permit the establishment of 
land-based 
facilities 
supporting 
off-
shore petroleum mining, processing, or 
distribution.

VITAL AND SUSTAINABLE RESOURCES 5
5.9 Coastal Resources
The City has three miles of coastline on the Pacific 
Ocean, intersected by three waterways that provide 
estuarine habitat. Offshore fisheries are supported 
by several federal and state-designated marine 
protected areas (MPAs) between Point Conception 
and the Mexican border. These fisheries support 
commercial and recreational fishing enterprises that 
operate out of the Oceanside Small Craft Harbor. 
The City’s highly developed coastline features the 
Oceanside Municipal Pier, the Oceanside Small Craft 
Harbor, the Junior Seau Amphitheater, two public 
parks, and The Strand – the only public roadway 
on the beachfront in San Diego County. Beachfront 
residential uses line the inland side of The Strand 
and extend to the City’s southern boundary. 
OCEANSIDE SMALL CRAFT HARBOR
The Oceanside Small Craft Harbor offers whale 
watching and sportfishing charters, kayak and small 
boat rentals, and a variety of retail and dining estab-
lishments. The harbor includes over 850 boat slips, 
85 of which provide for live-aboards.   
The Harbor is one of Oceanside’s many coastal fea-
tures that is vulnerable to coastal hazards, projected 
to become more severe under continued climate 
change and sea level rise. In the short term, 79 of 
the 100 acres of the Harbor fall within the poten-
tial future hazard zones, increasing to 86 acres in 
the mid-term and 93 acres in the long term (2100 
to 2140). Potential impacts of the expansion of 
coastal hazard zones include increased frequency 
of flooding and erosion, with associated water and 
flood damage; disrupted access to and from build-
ings and associated recreational and commercial 
services; and disrupted access and damage to boats 
and docks.
For more information on the Harbor and policies 
relating to public access, see the Healthy and 
Livable Community Element.
OCEANSIDE BEACHES
Oceanside has approximately 35 acres of usable 
beaches under the control of the City. These 
beaches are beloved by Oceanside residents and 
visitors alike; according to the 2018 Sports, Fitness, 
and Leisure Activities Topline Participation Report, 
visiting the beach is the number one outdoor recre-
ation activity in Oceanside. Approximately 54 per-
cent of Oceanside residents visit the beach at least 
once a week. 
Since the construction of the Camp Pendleton Boat 
Basin in 1942, Oceanside has experienced extensive 
beach erosion, as sand from the Santa Margarita 
River and other upcoast sources that would other-
wise replenish the City’s beaches is largely trapped 
behind the jetty and breakwater that protect the 
Boat Basin and the Oceanside Small Craft Harbor. 
As of 2023, less than a third of the City’s coastline 
provided dry sand areas, and nuisance flooding 
was common during storm and high tide events. 
Other factors contributing to beach loss include 
a highly developed coastline (which prevents 
the natural processes of bluff erosion and beach 
retreat), the damming and channelizing of the San

exploring various approaches to sand nourishment 
and retention. The City is following up this effort 
with an international design competition inviting 
innovative approaches to sourcing, distributing, and 
maintaining sand on the City’s beaches.
Much of the Oceanside shoreline relies on shoreline 
protection via seawalls or other armoring. Seawalls 
are the primary shoreline protective device from the 
northern City limits south to Tyson Street Park, and 
rip rap is the primary shoreline protective device 
from Tyson Street Park to the southern City limits.
Harbor Beach
Oceanside’s largest beach, Harbor Beach offers a 
variety of amenities including picnic areas, barbe-
cue grills, gazebos, and restrooms with showers, as 
well as three lifeguard towers. Harbor Beach also 
provides easy access to the Marina Inn Hotel and a 
variety of options for shopping and dining. Harbor 
Beach supplies several high-quality surf breaks, par-
ticularly near the harbor entrance. 
Harbor Beach is supported by a jetty located imme-
diately north of the mouth of the San Luis Rey River. 
While its ostensible purpose is to stabilize the river-
bank and keep the river mouth open to the ocean, 
this jetty also retains sand that would otherwise 
be transported downcoast by prevailing currents. 
Consequently, unlike other sand-starved stretches 
of the Oceanside coastline, Harbor Beach features 
more than 300 feet of dry sand extending inland 
from the water’s edge.
Breakwater Way Beach
This beach is located just south of Harbor Beach 
and the jetty on the north side of the San Luis 
Rey River. A persistent sandbar created by sed-
iment transfer from the river provides a good 
surf break. However, this beach is much narrower 
than Harbor Beach. Much of the inland edge of 
this beach is lined by The Strand, the only public 
beachfront roadway in San Diego County. Public 
amenities at Breakwater Way include showers, 
restrooms, picnic tables, barbecue grills, and a 
volleyball court. There are two public parking lots 
in the vicinity.
Tyson Street Beach and Park
Adjacent to the Oceanside Municipal Pier and the 
Junior Seau Amphitheater, Tyson Street Beach and 
Park is essentially an extension of the City’s revi-
talized downtown. Several resort-style hotels are 
located within walking distance of this beach. The 
pier produces consistent, high-quality surf breaks, 
making this area a popular spot for both profes-
sional and scholastic surfing competitions. In the 
summer, visitors to Tyson Beach can enjoy a wide 
range of food and retail concessions managed by 
MainStreet Oceanside. Other public amenities in 
this area include public restrooms and showers, 
covered picnic areas, play structures, and a police 
substation. This stretch of coastline is served by 
several public parking lots, including two that can 
be accessed from The Strand.    
Wisconsin Avenue Beach
Wisconsin Street Beach is located near the termi-
nus of The Strand at Wisconsin Street, which is an 
important coastal access roadway. As of 2023, this 


OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
5-56
highly-eroded beach provided no dry sand areas. 
During high tide events, the coastal revetment in 
this area is frequently overtopped by wave uprush, 
resulting in flooding and cobble projection on The 
Strand and an adjacent public parking lot. Beach 
access ramps through the coastal revetment in this 
area are in disrepair; signage encourages users to 
exercise caution when using these ramps and notes 
that users do so at their own risk.  
Beaches between Wisconsin Avenue 
and Oceanside Boulevard 
While street ends in this area (e.g., Hayes Street, 
Oceanside Boulevard) provide ample public access to 
the beachfront, as of 2023, this stretch of beach pro-
vided no dry sand, with the ocean extending into the 
coastal revetment on a daily basis. While this stretch 
of beachfront remains popular with the surfing com-
munity, it now draws far fewer beachgoers than it did 
a decade ago. Public parking in this area is available 
along South Pacific Street and other adjoining streets.
Buccaneer Beach
A small, family-oriented space popular with local 
residents, Buccaneer Beach serves as a transition 
point between higher density, tourist-oriented devel-
opment to the north and single-family development 
to the south.  This beach lies next to the mouth of 
Loma Alta Creek, the mouth of which is managed 
(pending permits in 2025) to lessen the likelihood 
of upstream flooding.  Additionally, the City’s Water 
Utilities Department operates an ultra-violet light 
water treatment system within the Loma Alta Slough 
to control water levels in the Slough by treating 
water and safely releasing it to the ocean.  If com-
pleted, the Loma Alta Slough Wetlands Enhancement 
Project will provide both carrying capacity and water 
quality improvements to the creek and adjacent 
beach. A walkway along the southern edge of Loma 
Alta Creek connects this beach to the Coast Highway 
corridor.  As of 2023, Buccaneer Beach had been 
reduced to a steep cobble bank by wave uprush and 
high tides.
BEACHES BETWEEN BUCCANEER AND 
THE CITY’S SOUTHERN BOUNDARY
As of 2023, this stretch of beachfront was largely 
devoid of dry sand areas, with the ocean extending 
into the coastal revetment on a daily basis. Public 
beach access in this area is somewhat limited, with 
only three accessways along its one-mile length. 
The most accommodating of these accessways 
lies at the terminus of Cassidy Street. This access-
way includes a viewing area and bicycle parking. 
The southernmost portion of this area is occupied 
by St. Malo, a gated single-family community that 
extends to the mouth of the Buena Vista Lagoon. 
Surrounded by water on three sides, this commu-
nity is among the most vulnerable to sea level rise 
and associated hazards.
Oceanside Municipal Pier
At 1,564 feet in length, the Oceanside Municipal 
Pier served as one of the longest piers on the west 
coast of the United States for many years.  Popular 
with residents and visitors alike, the pier anchors 
a stretch of beach that offers a variety of coastal 
amenities.  On April 25, 2025, the far west end of 
the pier caught fire, destroying the former Ruby’s 
Diner.  Once the west end is rebuilt, the pier has 
the ability to accommodate a restaurant use, fishing 
activities, a bait shop, lifeguard tower, and a series 
of viewing areas furnished with benches.  The City’s 
lifeguard operations center is nestled under the 
pier immediately seaward of The Strand.  The pier 
is connected to North Pacific Street by a concrete 
abutment comprised of twin conventionally rein-
forced bridges and a ramp down to the beach. The 
abutment is slated for repair.
THE STRAND
The Strand is the only public roadway in San Diego 
County that extends along the beachfront. The 
Strand serves pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists. 
Portions of The Strand are frequently inundated 
and subjected to wave runup and damage during

coastal storms or high-tide events due to its proxim-
ity to the coast and low elevation. South the Strand 
is the location of the future RE:BEACH Oceanside 
Pilot sand retention project and is expected to bring 
relief to nuisance flooding.  
CLIMATE CHANGE VULNERABILITY
Oceanside’s coastline and marine life is vulnerable to 
the pressures of climate change. Sea level rise exacer-
bates existing flood risks and provides the potential 
for more intense storms and damage along the coast. 
In the short term, 79 of the 100 acres of the Harbor 
fall within potential future hazard zones, increasing to 
86 acres in the mid-term and 93 acres in the long term 
(2100 to 2140). Potential impacts of the expansion of 
coastal hazard zones include increased frequency of 
flooding and erosion, with associated water and flood 
damage; disrupted access to and from buildings and 
associated recreational and commercial services; and 
disrupted access and damage to boats and docks.
Warming oceans that are more acidic and less oxy-
genated affect the reproduction and survival of 
marine species. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions 
in Oceanside is key to the protection of marine life 
and coastal resources and is addressed in detail in 
the City’s Climate Action Plan. In addition to the 
risks associated with human induced climate change, 
human activities can harm marine wildlife through 
boat collisions, excessive noise, harmful fishing prac-
tices, and pollution. One way to protect marine wild-
life from human-induced harms is to designate areas 
as national marine sanctuaries under the National 
Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), a 
designation that provides protections including speed 
limits, noise controls, and coordinated monitoring and 
management of marine resources. 
Oceanside’s coastline and marine resources are 
addressed in detail in the City’s Local Coastal Land 
Use Plan and the Local Coastal Program, state-man-
dated planning and implementation documents meant 
to demonstrate local consistency with the California 
Coastal Act (CCA). The CCA promotes public access 
to the coastline, visitor-serving uses, mitigation of 
coastal hazards, and preservation of scenic views, 
natural landforms, and biological resources. Updates 
to the City’s Local Coastal Land Use Plan and LCP are 
required to be completed by 2034 and will address 
issues of inundation of vulnerable areas and planning 
for future sea level rise.

GOALS AND POLICIES
GOALS
5-R 
The City will work with regulatory and 
resource agencies to achieve a balance 
between natural resources, economic ben-
efit, and recreational opportunities along 
the coastline, proactively planning for sea 
level rise, erosion, and other climate-related 
coastline changes under the guidance and 
requirements of the Coastal Commission 
and Ocean Protection Council. 
5-S 
The City will improve harbor infrastructure 
to support both recreational access, local 
commercial fishing operations, and low-
er-cost visitor accommodations.
5-T 
The City will prioritize beach restoration 
and preservation in the near term while 
acknowledging that other coastal adaptation 
strategies will be necessary to effectively 
address sea level rise and other climate-re-
lated impacts.

SAFE AND 
RESILIENT 
ENVIRONMENT 
Oceanside will be proactive and vigilant in 
mitigating risks associated with natural hazards, 
including those exacerbated by climate change. The City will 
discourage development in high-risk areas and require resilient site
          and building design in areas where new development is vulnerable to natural 
hazards.  Evacuation routes and protocols will ensure that community members 
can safely move out of harm’s way. Emphasis on infill and redevelopment in 
already urbanized areas will reduce development pressure on peripheral areas 
threatened by wildfire, landslides, and other potential natural disasters. The 
City will also assess and alleviate risks associated with industrial operations, 
the distribution and use of hazardous materials, crime, and social upheaval. The 
City will ensure adequate capacity for timely and effective emergency response.

OCEANSIDE GENERAL PLAN
6-4
6.1 Background
As a coastal community with a substantial wild-
land interface, floodplains, sloping terrain, farm-
land, and a variety of microclimates, Oceanside is 
exposed to a wide range of natural hazards that 
threaten public safety and the built environment. 
Additionally, as is true of any local jurisdiction, 
the Oceanside community is vulnerable to vari-
ous human-induced threats, including the release 
of hazardous materials, civil unrest, and crime. 
The Safe and Resilient Environment Element 
(SRE) assesses the City’s exposure to natural and 
human-induced hazards and outlines goals, pol-
icies, and actions designed to mitigate the risk 
of injury and property damage associated with 
these hazards.  
Wildfire is a relatively common occurrence in 
Oceanside, with the 2017 Lilac Fire being the 
most significant wildfire in recent history. The 
City’s highly eroded coastline is susceptible to 
wave uprush and inundation during king tides 
and high surf events; many beachfront homes 
and public facilities have been damaged by wave 
uprush and inundation in recent years. Properties 
adjacent to Loma Alta Creek experience flooding 
during major rain events, as do segments of State 
Route 78 in proximity to Buena Vista Creek. The 
segment of Coast Highway that crosses Buena 
Vista Lagoon can become impassable during 
major rain events. Droughts have threatened 
agricultural operations in the South Morro Hills 
area, where farmers struggle with the high cost 
of water. Landslides have damaged and destroyed 
single-family homes in Rancho del Oro and other 
neighborhoods. In short, much of Oceanside 
is vulnerable to natural hazards, with the City’s 
coastline, northern and eastern boundaries, hill-
sides, and areas near Loma Alta Creek and Buena 
Vista Creek and Lagoon being particularly at risk. 
Given that many of the physical conditions that 
present risk to life and property also contribute 
to community character, economic development, 
and quality of life, the SRE seeks to strike a bal-
ance between containment of natural hazards 
and preservation of natural features that provide 
ecological balance, recreational opportunities, a 
sense of openness, and a unique visual character. 
A fundamental goal of the SRE is to protect life 
and property without compromising the City’s 
ecological, recreational, and aesthetic assets.  
Oceanside’s location, climate, vegetation, and 
development patterns render the City vulnerable 
to riverine flooding, coastal storm and tidal events 
(exacerbated by sea level rise), wildfire, urban fire, 
and geologic and seismic hazards. Substantial 


6-5
SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
portions of the City, including the coastline and 
areas within historical riverine floodplains, are 
vulnerable to flooding, particularly during the 
winter rainy season. Further, Oceanside’s weath-
er, terrain, and dense vegetation at its boundaries 
bring increased fire risk to the area. Areas along 
the City’s interface with Marine Corp Base Camp 
Pendleton, the unincorporated communities 
of Fallbrook and Bonsall, and the cities of Vista 
and Carlsbad contain designated Very High Fire 
Hazard Severity zones. Like most of Southern 
California, the community is also considered 
seismically active and susceptible to earthquakes 
resulting from fault movement. Strong seismic 
ground shaking and earthquake-induced lique-
faction and/or landslides are the primary geologic 
hazards of concern in Oceanside.
In the face of climate change and increasing risk 
of flooding, coastal storms and extreme tides, 
urban heat, fire, and geologic hazards, Oceanside 
is required by State law to develop General Plan 
goals and policies that serve to minimize its vul-
nerability to these phenomena and ensure ade-
quate emergency response in the event of natural 
disaster. A resilient community is one that is both 
proactive in identifying and warding off natural 
hazards and prepared to address the impacts 
of before has put in place both preventive and 
responsive measures. Although many of these 
hazards affect Oceanside at a citywide scale, the 
impacts of climate change and associated envi-
ronmental and public safety hazards may be more 
profound in certain areas, raising questions about 
environmental justice. While the most vulnera-
ble properties in Oceanside tend to be situated 
in higher-income neighborhoods (e.g., beach-
front, estate residential near the City’s northern 
and eastern boundaries), there are less affluent 
populations in the North Valley and Capistrano 
Neighborhood Planning Areas that face the 
threat of wildfire with limited evacuation routes. 
There is also farmworker housing in South Morro 
Hills in close proximity to a State-designated high 
fire hazard severity zone. In light of threats facing 
low-resource communities in Oceanside, the SRE 
includes goals and policies that call upon the City 
to view natural hazards through the lens of envi-
ronmental justice.
PURPOSE AND INTENT
The Safe and Resilient Environment (SRE) Element 
outlines Oceanside’s vulnerability to natural and 
human-made hazards and presents a framework 
for minimizing risks to life and property. Topics 
addressed include:
• Hydrological Hazards
• Fire
• Geologic and Seismic Hazards
• Climate Change 
• Airport Hazards
• Emergency Preparedness and Response
• Human Induced Hazards
Each section of the SRE contains an overview of a 
specific hazard or safety-related issue, a summary 
of local populations vulnerable to the hazard(s) in 
question, an outline of the existing institutional 
support system (e.g., relevant agencies, regula-
tions, and programs), and a set of hazard-specific 
goals and policies. Relevant actions are collected 
at the end of the Element.
The City’s exposure to environmental hazards is 
also addressed in the San Diego County’s 2023 
Multi-Jurisdictional 
Hazard 
Mitigation 
Plan 
(MJHMP). The MJHMP is a countywide plan 
that identifies risks and strategies for minimiz-
ing damage from natural and human-induced 
disasters. The plan is a comprehensive resource 
document that serves to enhance local policies 
for hazard mitigation and provide inter-jurisdic-
tional coordination. The MJHMP also includes 
an “annex” for Oceanside – prepared by City 
staff – that identifies the City’s principal hazards 
and outlines specific actions the City intends 
to take to mitigate these hazards. The principal 
hazards identified in the City’s MJHMP annex 
include wildfire, riverine and coastal flooding, 
drought, landslide, earthquake, and extreme heat 
events. City disciplines responsible for mitigation 
measures outlined in the annex include Water 
Utilities, Public Works, Fire, and Development 
Services. The MJHMP is available for review on 
the County’s website at: https://www.sandiego-
county.gov/oes/emergency_management/oes_jl_
mitplan.html.

6-6
Additionally, Oceanside’s Climate Action Plan 
(CAP) promulgates a variety of GHG emissions 
reduction measures that, combined with federal, 
state, and regional climate action efforts, seek to 
reduce the adverse impacts of climate change. 
Originally adopted in 2019, the CAP has since 
been updated in conjunction with the prepara-
tion of the SRE and other General Plan elements. 
The City intends to adaptively manage, update 
and modify the CAP at regular five year intervals.  
STATE REQUIREMENTS (NATURAL HAZ-
ARDS, CLIMATE ADAPTATION, ENVI-
RONMENTAL JUSTICE)
California Government Code Section 65302(g) 
requires general plans to include a Safety Element 
to identify and address hazards for the protection 
of the local community. In accordance with State 
law, the SRE addresses seismic and geologic-re-
lated hazards, flood hazards, wildland and fire 
hazards, evacuation routes, hazardous materials, 
and other related topics.
Passed in 2016, SB 379 requires that, begin-
ning January 1, 2017, all cities and counties in 
California include climate adaptation and resilien-
cy strategies in their updated safety elements.1 
Climate adaptation must be addressed with goals, 
policies, and actions informed by a climate change 
vulnerability assessment, as well as specific 
actions meant to reduce the community’s vulner-
ability to natural hazards exacerbated by climate 
change. Per SB 379, cities and counties that have 
prepared and adopted Local Hazard Mitigation 
Plans (LHMPs) and/or Climate Adaptation Plans 
(CAPs) that address climate adaptation can ref-
erence and summarize these climate adaptation 
planning efforts in their updated safety elements.  
In accordance with State law, the SRE’s goals 
and policies incorporate climate adaptation and 
resilience measures and are informed by San 
Diego County’s MJHMP. The MJHMP for the San 
Diego County Planning Area was developed in 
accordance with the Disaster Mitigation Act of 
2000 (DMA 2000) and followed FEMA’s Local 
Hazard Mitigation Plan guidance. The MJHMP 
incorporates a process where hazards are iden-
tified and profiled, the people and facilities at 
1  Jackson, Hannah-Beth. SB-379 Land use: general plan: 
safety element., Government Code § 65302 (2015). 
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.
xhtml?bill_id=201520160SB379
risk are analyzed, and mitigation actions are 
developed to reduce or eliminate hazard risk. 
The implementation of these mitigation actions, 
which include both short and long-term strate-
gies, involve planning, policy changes, programs, 
projects, and other activities. Further, as noted 
above, the City’s annex to the County MJHMP 
identifies top hazards threatening the jurisdiction 
as well as appropriate jurisdictional-level goals, 
objectives, and action items. The City’s annex to 
the County MJHMP is meant to be a more near 
term and living document that will be annually 
reviewed and updated per the County’s new pro-
tocol. While the SRE provides an overview of the 
environmental and human-induced hazards that 
affect Oceanside, the MJHMP provides greater 
analysis, context, and mitigation strategies for 
these hazards. As such, it is not appropriate to 
reiterate the detailed strategies of Oceanside’s 
annex of the MJHMP in the SRE which is meant 
to serve as a high-level and long-range plan.
California Government Code Section 65040.12(e) 
defines “environmental justice” as “… the fair 
treatment and meaningful involvement of people 
of all races, cultures, incomes, and national ori-
gins with respect to the development, adoption, 
implementation, and enforcement of environ-
mental laws, regulations, and policies.” Adopted 
in 2016, Senate Bill 1000 requires that local juris-
dictions that include qualifying disadvantaged

communities address environmental justice in

6.2 Hydrological 
Hazards
STORM-INDUCED FLOODING 
Flooding is the inundation of normally dry land 
as a result of a rise in the level of surface waters 
or the rapid accumulation of stormwater runoff; 
it becomes a hazard when the flow of water has 
the potential to damage property and threaten 
human life or health. Substantial portions of the 
Planning Area, including the immediate coastal 
boundary and areas within historic floodplains, 
can be affected by flooding, particularly during 
the winter rainy season. The City encompasses 
approximately 42 square miles and is divided into 
four major watersheds (San Luis Rey, Loma Alta, 
Buena Vista, and Agua Hedionda). Most of the 
Oceanside drains to waterways that flow to the 
Pacific Ocean.4 Consequently, the City is exposed 
to both riverine and coastal flooding, particular-
ly when major rain events coincide with storm 
surge, large swells, and extreme high tides.
Riverine flooding occurs when streams and rivers 
exceed the capacity of their channels to accom-
modate flow and crest their banks, spilling out 
into adjacent land. A levee system along the 
San Luis Rey River, installed by the Army Corps 
of Engineers in the early 1990s, has significant-
ly reduced flood risk in the San Luis Rey Valley. 
Currently, the most flood-prone waterway in the 
city is Loma Alta Creek, which has been hemmed 
in by development and expansion of the railroad 
that was constructed along the Loma Alta valley in 
the early 1900s. Rainfall is the main contributing 
4  City of Oceanside, Master Plan of Drainage Update 2013, 
October 2013, https://www.ci.oceanside.ca.us/civicax/
filebank/blobdload.aspx?blobid=44657. 
factor to flooding, thought the impact of rain-
fall is contingent upon soil moisture conditions 
before the storm, the extent of urban develop-
ment and impervious surfaces, and water levels 
in the upstream reservoirs.5 
Coastal flooding is usually the result of a large 
storm and/or high tides. Floodwaters are driven 
ashore by high winds, an event known as storm 
surge. High velocity wave action and extreme 
tides can cause significant damage to coast-
al development and infrastructure. With a 
west-facing coastline exposed to the open ocean, 
the City experiences large swells throughout the 
year and extreme tides in early summer and early 
winter. Many beachfront residential properties 
in Oceanside experience regular overtopping of 
shoreline protective devices, which erodes pri-
vate and public beach areas, undermines hard-
scape, and occasionally pushes seawater into 
inland areas.
Flood Hazard Zones 
According to the County’s MJHMP, FEMA FIRM 
data was used to determine hazard risk for floods 
in the county. FEMA defines flood risk primari-
ly by a 100-year flood zone, which is applied to 
those areas with a 1 percent chance, on average, 
of flooding in any given year. Any area that lies 
within the FEMA-designated 100-year floodplain 
is designated as high risk. Any area found in the 
500-year floodplain is designated at low risk. 
Base flood elevations (BFE) were also used in the 
flood hazard modeling process. A BFE is the ele-
vation of the water surface resulting from a flood 
that has a 1 percent chance of occurring in any 
given year (i.e., the height of the base flood).
Based on FEMA Records, the San Diego region 
has not suffered severe repetitive loss (residen-
tial properties that have at least four NFIP pay-
ments over $5,000 each with the cumulative 
claim exceeding $20,000 or at least two separate 
claims payments with the cumulative amount 
exceeding the market value of the building) since 
1974. However, in Oceanside, there have been 15 
repetitive losses (losses of at least $1,000 each). 
Based on the historical record, the likelihood of 
flooding in the city is highly likely.

Figure 6-1: Flood Hazards  


Figure 6-1 displays the location and extent of 
flood hazard areas for the City of Oceanside. 
Several portions of the city are subject to a 100-
year flood, meaning a flood with a one percent 
chance of occurring in any given year. As shown in 
the figure, high hazard (100-year floodway) zones 
in the city are generally concentrated within the 
coastal and riverine areas. Major watershed areas 
connecting the local mountain range to the coast-
al region, such as the North Valley and San Luis 
Rey, show several 100-year flood hazard areas. 
Flash flooding is also more common in these 
areas. To mitigate such flood hazards in riverine 
areas, the City works in consultation with the 
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on the San Luis Rey 
River Flood Control Project. The U.S. Army Corps 
of Engineer’s San Luis Rey Flood Control Project 
is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at reduc-
ing flood risks in the City, particularly along the 
San Luis Rey River. The City collaborates with the 
Corps on the project and shares costs and main-
tenance responsibility for the project’s implemen-
tation. The City’s Public Works Department per-
forms annual vegetation management activities 
in the project area, which consists of 7.2 miles of 
channelized and un-channelized reaches of the 
San Luis Rey River.
TSUNAMI AND SEICHE 
A tsunami is a series of high-energy waves that 
radiate outward like pond ripples from an area 
where a generating event occurs, arriving at 
shorelines over an extended period. Tsunamis 
can be induced by earthquakes, landslides, and 
submarine volcanic explosions. According to the 
County’s 2017 MJHMP, the impact of tsunamis on 
the San Diego coastline has been low, but inunda-
tion maps developed by the California Office of 
Emergency Services and the California Geologic 
Survey show the potential for moderate damage 
along low-lying areas. The largest tsunami effect 
recorded in San Diego since 1950 was May 22, 
1960, when an earthquake off the coast of Chile 
generated maximum wave heights of 2.1 feet. In 
this event, 80 meters of dock were destroyed, and 
a barge sunk in Quivera Basin.6 
According to mapping produced in the MJHMP, 
the highest risk zones in San Diego County are 
located within the coastal zone. The entirety of 
Oceanside’s coastline is designated as a VE Zone, 
which is defined by FEMA as the coastal area sub-
ject to a velocity hazard (wave action). Further, 
maximum tsunami runup is projected to extend 
up the San Luis Rey River to the vicinity of the 
Oceanside Municipal Airport, landward of Coast 
Highway where this roadway crosses Loma Alta 
Creek and Buena Vista Lagoon. In the City’s coast-
al area, a total of 790 residents as well as 1,265 
residential and 198 commercial buildings could be 
exposed to a tsunami.7 This map, prepared by the 
Bureau of Land Management, shows areas within 
the City that would be impacted by maximum tsu-
nami runup.
The greatest type of tsunami risk in San Diego 
County is material damage to small watercraft, 
harbors, and some waterfront structures, with 
flooding along the coast. While the likelihood of 
large-scale devastation in Oceanside resulting 
6  County of San Diego, Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard

sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/oes/emergency_
management/HazMit/2018/2018%20Hazard%20
Mitigation%20Plan.pdf.
7  County of San Diego, Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard 
Mitigation Plan, October 2017, https://www.

from tsunamis appears to be relatively small, the 
Oceanside Small Craft Harbor and other coastal 
amenities could be significantly impacted. In the 
harbor, boat docks could be lifted off of pilings 
that currently hold them in place, Harbor Drive 
and other perimeter roadways could be inundat-
ed, and various marine safety facilities and public 
amenities could be damaged.  
Oceanside is a TsunamiReady Community, as 
designated by the National Weather Service. 
The City earned this designation by defining 
tsunami hazard zones, installing evacuation 
route signage, conducting outreach on tsunami 
risk, establishing alert systems, and preparing a 
formal tsunami operations plan. This map shows 
the 42-foot run-up zone calculated by the State 
Office of Emergency Services and the University 
of Southern California, Tsunami Research Group.8 
Signed evacuation routes within this zone include 
Surfrider Way, Seagaze Drive, Wisconsin Avenue,

Early warning of an approaching tsunami and clear-
ance of high-risk areas are essential to minimizing 
the likelihood of injury and loss of life. The City’s 
public safety departments have established proto-
cols for alerting and evacuating community mem-
bers from tsunami hazard zones.
A seiche is a resonant, side-to-side movement of 
water in a closed or mostly closed body of water 
such as the San Francisco Bay. The USGS defines 
a seiche as the sloshing of a closed body of water 
which can be caused from earthquake shaking. 
Unlike tsunamis, which are created by the sudden 
uplift of the sea floor, seismic seiches are stand-
ing waves that occur when an earthquake passes 
through the area. In San Diego County, the 
only threat of large-scale damage from seiches 
appears to come from localized or downstream 
flooding that would be caused by large volumes 
of water overtopping a dam or reservoir.9 Thus, 
the likelihood of large-scale devastation in 
Oceanside resulting from seiches is minimal.

DAM FAILURE AND INUNDATION
Many dam failures in the United States have 
been secondary results of other disasters. The 
most common causes are earthquakes, land-
slides, extreme storms, equipment malfunction, 
structural damage, foundation failures, and sab-
otage. Poor construction, lack of maintenance 
and repair, and deficient operational procedures 
are preventable or correctable by a program of 
regular inspections. Terrorism and vandalism are 
serious concerns for which all operators of public 
facilities must plan. Given the evolving nature of 
such threats, they are under continuous review 
by public safety agencies. 
In San Diego County, most dams are greater than 
50 years old and are characterized by increased 
hazard potential due to downstream develop-
ment and increased risk due to structural deteri-
oration and inadequate spillway capacity.10
The California Department of Water Resources’ 
Division of Safety of Dams reviews and approves 
inundation maps for extremely high, high, and sig-
nificant hazard dams. As detailed in the County’s 
MJHMP, there are no dams in Oceanside that 
present a significant downstream hazard risk. 
However, located outside the City at the south-
east base of Mount Palomar and at the head-
waters of the San Luis Rey River watershed, the 
10 County of San Diego, Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard 
Mitigation Plan, October 2017, https://www.
sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/oes/emergency_
management/HazMit/2018/2018%20Hazard%20
Mitigation%20Plan.pdf.
Lake Henshaw Dam has the potential to flood 
several portions of Oceanside as shown in Figure 
6-2. If Lake Henshaw were to fail, 4,775 acres 
of the Planning Area could be flooded. Figure 
6-2 depicts the dam breach inundation areas for 
Oceanside, which occur in areas adjacent to the 
San Luis Rey River. 
The risks posed by dam failures, particularly 
Lake Henshaw Dam, are mitigated by the regu-
latory safeguards in place. The Vista Irrigation 
District (VID) is responsible for assessing and 
maintaining Lake Henshaw Dam. According to 
a 2022 report from the California Department 
of Water Resources Division of Safety of Dams, 
the Lake Henshaw Dam is in ‘Satisfactory’ con-
dition, meaning that no existing or potential dam 
safety deficiencies are recognized.11 As part of 
VID’s 2020 Urban Water Management Plan, the 
district developed goals and objectives to reduce 
the possibility of damage and losses from dam 
failure. Specific interventions include updat-
ing dam inundation plans regularly, identifying 
hazard-prone structures, constructing barriers 
around structures, encouraging structural retro-
fitting, and coordinating with the U.S. Army Corps 
of Engineers, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, and 
the California Department of Water Resources to 
support existing efforts to mitigate dam failure.

SEA LEVEL RISE
Oceanside is bordered to the west by three miles 
of Pacific Ocean coastline. While the coast is an 
important biological, cultural, recreational, and 
economic resource, it also poses an environ-
mental risk to residents, visitors, and properties 
located near the waterfront. Sea level rise (SLR), 
the rise in global sea level accompanying other 
effects of global climate change, has already 
increased water levels measured at a station in La 
Jolla at a rate of six inches over the last century.12 
As sea levels rise further due to global warming, it 
will increase the flooding hazard from the ocean, 
especially during storm events. 
Both private property and public facilities on the 
City’s beachfront experience wave uprush and 
inundation on a regular basis, particularly during 
high surf and king tide events. While most of these 
impacts have thus far been minor and temporary, 
some properties and facilities have sustained sig-
nificant damage. Additionally, sinkholes, under-
mined beach access ramps, and unstable revet-
ment have created public safety hazards.
The County’s MJHMP projects up to two feet of 
sea level rise by mid-century. For five feet of SLR 
(Figure 6-3), which represents an intermediate 
to high end-of-century SLR scenario,13 the City’s 
exposure to 100-year coastal flooding is signifi-
cantly greater relative to current conditions, with 
the beachfront and estuarine areas being partic-
ularly vulnerable. In 2019, the City prepared a 
Coastal Hazards Vulnerability Assessment (VA), 
which illustrates how coastal properties and 
assets would be impacted under various sea level 
rise scenarios. Existing shoreline protective devic-
es along the beachfront may not be adequate to 
withstand an additional two feet of sea-level rise; 
without enhanced protection, many beachfront 
properties and assets could become increasingly 
vulnerable to frequent wave uprush and potential 
damage.
12 California Environmental Protection Agency and Office 
of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, 2013. 
“Indicators of Climate Change in California.”
13 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 
“Sea Level Rise Viewer”, 2023, https://coast.noaa.gov/
digitalcoast/tools/slr.html. 
Recent studies suggest a narrower range of pro-
jected global, national, and regional sea level 
rise at mid-century than previously reported. 
The 2022 National Oceanic and Atmospheric 
Administration (NOAA) report, Global and 
Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United 
States, provides updated mean projections and 
extreme water level probabilities along U.S coast-
lines.14 According to the report, relative sea level 
along the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) coastline is 
expected to rise on average of 0.8-1.0 feet over 
the next 30 years (2020–2050). The 2100 scenar-
io projections of relative sea level rise along the 
CONUS coastline are about 2.0–7.2 feet. With 
increasingly accurate sea level rise projection 
scenarios, local jurisdictions can further devel-
op proactive solutions to mitigate and adapt to 
changing coastlines from sea level rise. 
Sea level rise will continue to exacerbate impacts 
associated other events that temporarily increase 
sea level – e.g., high astronomical tides, strong 
winds, high surf, storm surge, and thermoexpan-
sion, and thermo-expansion created by phenom-
ena like El Nino. San Diego County’s shoreline will 
see increasingly more hours of high sea levels as 
the century progresses. High sea level events are 
defined as the 99.99th percentile hourly sea level 
calculated for the period of 1970-1999. These 
high sea levels are caused by factors including 
high astronomical tides, wind, waves, and storm 
surges. In the present climate, San Diego expe-
riences an average of one hour of high sea level 
per year. By 2030, high sea levels are expected to 
occur 12 hours per year on average. By mid-cen-
tury, this increases to 62 hours per year. These 
high sea levels put natural ecosystems (beaches, 
cliffs, wetlands) and development at risk of expo-
sure to flooding and wave action.15

6-16
SOCIAL VULNERABILITY 
Flood hazards, dam breach inundation areas, 
and sea level rise impacts in the City are gen-
erally concentrated within the coastal and riv-
erine areas. As illustrated in maps included in 
Oceanside General Plan Update Background 
Report #2, lower-income areas may be particu-
larly affected by flooding hazards. The Townsite 
neighborhood in Oceanside contains a high-pov-
erty census tract, parts of which may be at risk of 
damage from coastal flooding and sea level rise. 
Mobile home parks adjacent to Loma Alta Creek, 
which accommodate many lower-income house-
holds, are vulnerable to both coastal and riverine 
flooding. Two recreational vehicle parks adjacent 
to Loma Alta Creek, both of which qualify as low-
cost visitor-serving accommodations, also face 
significant flood risk.
Vulnerable populations (e.g., poor, elderly, chil-
dren, and unhoused individuals) may also live in 
areas that are more prone to flooding and envi-
ronmental pollution. Flooding can compromise 
existing infrastructure, health services, and 
contaminate inundated areas with hazardous 
substances which leads to exacerbated health 
impacts on vulnerable groups. Further, unhoused 
populations may lack a secure place to shelter 
during a flood, and they are often more difficult 
to reach via emergency alert systems.16 
Goals and policies developed by the City will work 
to mitigate flooding and sea level rise hazards, 
while prioritizing adaptation for socially-vulnera-
ble groups through the development of local poli-
cies and programs consistent with state guidance. 
Such policies will foster community and regional 
engagement for sea level rise planning. Coupled 
with policies on future sea level rise monitoring, 
findings from these engagement efforts will help 
the City establish planning thresholds for new 
development, sea level rise adaptation strate-
gies, and other coastal adaptation measures. As 
for existing policies and protocols, climate adap-
tation strategies called out in Oceanside’s sec-
tion of the MJHMP include the development of 
an audio warning system to notify residents of 
flooding and the identification of financial assis-
tance programs to fund flood mitigation projects. 
16 Thomas, K., Hardy RD., Lazrus H., Mendez M., Orlove 
B., Rivera-Collazo, I., Roberts JT., Rockman M., Warner 
BP., Winthrop R., Explaining differential vulnerability 
to climate change: A social science review (December 
2018). Oct 29 2019: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/
full/10.1002/wcc.565.

SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
INSTITUTIONAL AND REGULATORY 
FRAMEWORK 
FEMA is responsible for managing the 100-year 
floodplain, areas with a one percent or greater 
chance of flooding in any given year. A Flood 
Insurance Rate Map, an official FEMA-prepared 
map, delineates both Special Flood Hazard Areas 
(the 100-year floodplain) and flood-risk premium 
zones (as shown in Figure 6-3). FEMA adminis-
ters the National Flood Insurance Program, which 
includes floodplain management and flood hazard 
mapping and provides subsidized flood insurance 
to communities that comply with FEMA regula-
tions to limit development in floodplains. Under 
Executive Order 11988, FEMA requires local 
governments covered by the National Flood 
Insurance Program to pass and enforce a flood-
plain management ordinance that specifies min-
imum requirements for any construction within 
the 100-year floodplain. 
Current state guidance calls for preparing for 
at least 3.5 feet of sea level rise by 2050.17 To 
prepare for this extent of sea level rise, adapta-
tion strategies are incorporated into the goals 
and policies of the SRE. The City has begun to 
address how its shoreline can be rendered more 
resilient to sea level rise in the future. The City 
17 California Ocean Protection Council, 2020. Strategic Plan 
to Protect California’s Coast and Ocean 2020-2025
is currently updating its Local Coastal Program 
(LCP), a planning document that regulates devel-
opment in the City’s Coastal Zone in accordance 
with the California Coastal Act. The updated LCP 
will assess existing and future conditions in the 
City’s coastal zone, establish new policies and 
strategies for coastal adaptation, and amend 
zoning standards to require resilient building 
design and materials on at-risk properties. 
Priority actions for the City of Oceanside iden-
tified in the Local Coastal Program Update 
planning process enhance and improve coastal 
access, encourage and manage coastal devel-
opment, protect and enhance scenic resources 
and public views, protect and restore natural 
resources, reduce risks from coastal hazards, 
and protect archaeological, paleontological, and 
cultural resources. The SRE incorporates these 
priority actions in its goals and policies to ensure 
implementation is occurring in an efficient and 
appropriate manner. Under uncertain future cli-
mate change scenarios, protecting shorelines and 
adapting to sea level rise will need to continue 
to be an iterative process that requires commu-
nity coordination and guidance. See the following 
Climate Change section in this element for more 
information regarding future climate change 
projections.

6-18
RESPONSIBLE AGENCIES 
There are several agencies responsible for flood 
management and emergency response in the San 
Diego region. The SRE emphasizes interagency 
coordination and planning efforts between the 
City of Oceanside and the following agencies to 
best mitigate and adapt to flooding and sea level 
rise. 
The California Department of Water Resources 
engages in flood management and flood emer-
gency response programs. It developed the Flood 
Emergency Response Information Exchange 
to improve flood emergency preparedness, 
response, and recovery. 
San Diego Regional Water Quality Control 
Board. The San Diego Regional Water Quality 
Control Board enforces waterway protection 
and pollution control regulations in Oceanside. 
The San Diego Water Board regulates discharg-
es from Phase I municipal separate storm sewer 
systems (MS4s / City-owned storm drains) in 
the San Diego Region under the Regional MS4 
Permit. The permit has provisions that requires 
municipalities to implement low impact devel-
opment hydrology designs for projects within its 
land use planning authority. 
The San Diego County Flood Control District 
(FCD) deals with watershed issues in the 
Unincorporated County of San Diego, focusing 
primarily on flood control issues. The FCD is to 
provide for the control of the flood and storm 
waters of the district, and of the flood and storm 
waters that flow into the district. 
The Oceanside Fire Department (OFD) is the 
primary agency responsible for responding to, 
recovering from, and mitigating against any 
hazard that affects the City of Oceanside. OFD’s 
mission is to meet and exceed community needs 
and expectations through the preservation and 
protection of life, property, and the environment.

SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
GOALS AND POLICIES
GOALS 
6-A 
People, property, and natural resources 
will be protected from riverine flooding 
through land use regulation, flood 
control measures, and community 
awareness initiatives.
6-B 
Flood control measures will be balanced 
with efforts to enhance the ecological, 
recreational, and aesthetic values of the 
City’s waterways.
6-C 
The potential impacts of sea level rise 
and associated coastal hazards will be 
minimized through proactive planning 
and timely action.
POLICIES
Flooding Hazards
6-1 
Balance the use of waterways and flood-
plains for multiple purposes, with empha-
sis on public safety and environmental 
protection. Potentially appropriate uses 
in the floodplains include:
• Flood control 
• Groundwater recharge
• Open space
• Natural habitat 
• Nature study
• Pedestrian, equestrian, and bicycle 
activity
• Passive and active recreational activity
6-2 
Where buffers are required between 
development and waterways, explore 
opportunities for both habitat restoration 
and passive-use recreational amenities 
within these buffers, in context of policies 
within the Vital & Sustainable Resources 
Element.
6-3 
Update development standards to require 
flood-resilient design on properties 
subject to significant flood risk.
6-4 
Continue to update flood risk mitigation 
strategies and standards to adapt to 
climate change induced sea level rise and 
increased risk of flooding. 
6-5 
Update the City’s Master Drainage Plan.
6-6 
Undertake nature-based strategies to 
restore waterways, improve stormwater 
infiltration, recharge aquifers, support 
biodiversity, improve water quality, 
and increase access to natural spaces. 
Prioritize green infrastructure over grey 
infrastructure wherever feasible.
6-7 
Ensure that new construction and major 
improvements to existing structures 
within flood zones are in compliance with 
federal requirements, in part to ensure 
ongoing participation in the National 
Flood Insurance Program (NFIP).
6-8 
Prohibit development in FEMA-
delineated floodways; ensure that all new 
development in 100-year floodplains 
is elevated at least one foot above 
base flood elevation and ensure FIMA 
maps are updated with Letters of Map 
Revisions accordingly. 
6-9 
Develop a tracking system to identify 
responsibility for the maintenance 
of flood control facilities (e.g., public 
and private detention basins). Monitor 
and enforce the maintenance of such 
facilities annually to ensure they remain 
in good repair and are able to serve their 
intended purpose.
6-10 
Work with property owners, residents of 
mobile home parks, and other stakehold-
ers to develop cohesive areawide flooding 
prevention strategies in high-risk areas, 
including coastal and riverine areas.
6-11 
Continue to coordinate with FEMA, the 
Army Corps of Engineers, the San Diego 
County Flood Control District (FCD), 
and the State Division of Safety of Dams 
on flood-control-related projects and 
floodplain modeling updates.

Tsunami Hazards
6-19

evacuation zone, require use of low 
impact engineering techniques, such as 
elevating structures above projected 
water levels, to mitigate impacts to 
people and property.

Office of Emergency Services to ensure 
the City receives timely warnings of 
potential tsunamis.
6-21 
Ensure that educational materials about 
tsunami preparation and response are 
readily available and up to date. 
6-22 
Review the Tsunami Emergency 
Evacuation Plans every several years 
to address any significant changes to 
conditions within tsunami hazard zones. 
Solicit and integrate community into this 
review process.

SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
6.3 Fire Hazards
WILDFIRE/WILDFIRE URBAN INTERFACE
Wildfire has become an increasing occurrence in 
California. A wildfire is any uncontrolled fire on 
undeveloped land that requires fire suppression. 
According to the County’s MJHMP, wildfires are 
common in San Diego County, with large historic 
wildfires recorded in 2003 and 2007. In October 
2003, the Cedar Fire caused 17 deaths and 
destroyed 332,766 acres of land, 3,239 structures, 
and cost approximately 450 million dollars. San 
Diego County’s worst wildfire complex occurred 
in October 2007, known as the Witch Creek and 
Guejito Fires. At the height of the firestorm there 
were seven fires burning within the county. The 
fires destroyed 369,000 acres (13 percent of the 
County), 2,670 structures, 239 vehicles, and two 
commercial properties. There were 10 civilian 
deaths, 23 civilian injuries, and 10 firefighter inju-
ries with the cost of the fire exceeding 1.5 billion 
dollars. In total, wildfires have prompted nine 
Proclaimed States of Emergency in the County of 
San Diego between 1950-2014.  
Recent wildfires in San Diego County have also 
resulted in significant structure loss. The May 
2014 San Diego County Wildfires resulted in 
26,000 acres burned and 65 structures destroyed. 
In June 2016, the Border Fire resulted in 7,609 
acres burned and two deaths. In December 2017, 
the Lilac Fire left 4,100 acres burned and 157 
structures destroyed. In September 2020, the 
Valley Fire resulted in 16,390 acres burned and 
66 structures destroyed. In May 2022, a brush 
fire burned nearly 660 acres of vegetation at 
Camp Pendleton, which is located just north of 
Oceanside. In addition to direct impacts, major 
wildfires that occur outside Oceanside still have 
profound effects on economies, health, and eco-
system function throughout the region.  
State law requires the California Department 
of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE), to 
identify areas, or zones, of very high fire hazard 
severity potential under the Fire and Resources 
Assessment Program (FRAP). These Fire Hazard 
Severity Zones (FHSZ) are mapped and identified 
based on expected burn probabilities, potential 
fuels over a 30- to 50-year time period, and their 
correlated expected fire behavior, in order to 
better predict possible vegetation fire exposure 
to buildings and developments. According to 
FRAP mapping shown in Figure 6-4, the north-
west portion of Oceanside along the San Luis Rey 
River, including the airport and just north of it, 
is designated by CAL FIRE as a Very High Fire 
Hazard Severity Zone (VHFHSZ). In addition, a 
small southern portion of Oceanside, including 
Ocean Hills and just north of Calavera Lake, is 
designated as a VHFHSZ. These VHFHSZs are 
considered Local Responsibility Areas (LRA), 
where local governments have fiscal responsi-
bility for wildfire protection. The Oceanside Fire 
Department (OFD) Fire Station 7 and Fire Station 
4 service these VHFHSZs in the city. The east-
ern portion of the city is also adjacent to State 
Responsibility Areas (SRAs), where the State has 
responsibility for wildfire protection, designated

SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
from Moderate to Very High Fire Hazard Severity 
Zones. There are approximately 2,592 acres of 
land mapped as VHFHSZ within the Planning 
Area according to CAL FIRE representing approx-
imately four percent of land area in the city limits.
Additionally, the northern boundary of the 
Planning Area adjacent to Camp Pendleton is 
largely defined as part of the wildland-urban inter-
face (WUI) as well as areas south and west of the 
city limits. The wildland-urban interface (WUI) is 
an area where structures and other human devel-
opment meets or intermingles with undeveloped 
wildlands. This designation is based on the fuel 
load, weather, and terrain factors that influence 
fire likelihood and fire behavior. The mapped WUI 
includes these areas mapped as VHFHSZ. While 
many of the fires in the WUI are small and can be 
controlled, the proximity of dense residential com-
munities to areas that are fire prone increases the 
hazard of wildfire in Oceanside. Wildfire is a grow-
ing threat to development at the edges of urban 
areas. As climate change brings longer, hotter 
summers and more severe droughts, wildfires are 
becoming more extensive and severe. The risk of 
wildfire is greatest on the City’s edges and other 
areas where vegetation is densest: along the Camp 
Pendleton boundary, urban canyons throughout 
the city, and the San Luis Rey River. In addition, 
VHFHSVs are influencing the insurance coverage 
crisis for Oceanside’s homeowners and businesses 
which is a critical socioeconomic threat linked to a 
changing climate.
There are a significant number of structures that 
are vulnerable to wildfire in the city. The California 
State Building and Fire code, most recently updat-
ed in 2022, requires minimum standards be met 
for new buildings in fire hazard severity zones. The 
update to the code brings notable changes, such 
as detailed requirements for fire-resistance-rated 
construction and fire sprinkler systems. Almost 
all housing in the city—about 96 percent—was 
built prior to 2010 and may not meet standards 
established in recent Fire Code amendments.18 
It is unknown how many of these structures are 
18 United States Census Bureau, 2020: American 
Community Survey 5-Year Estimates Subject 
Tables – Year Structure Built (B25034) https://d 
ata.census.gov/table?q=housing+year+built&g 
=1600000US0653322&tid=ACSDT5Y2020.B25034.
in fire hazard zones. As outlined in the MJHMP, 
more than 50 percent of the City’s building inven-
tory faces some risk from wildfire. In addition, an 
estimated number of 21 critical facilities in the 
city are in wildfire risk areas, resulting in upwards 
of 530 million dollars of critical facility damage. 
These facilities could have a significant amount 
of functional downtime after a wildfire, creating 
not only a need for mitigation but also a need for 
continuity of operations planning to develop pro-
cedures for providing services without access to 
critical facilities.
In conjunction with the County’s 2023 MJHMP, 
the City of Oceanside has developed several wild-
fire-related goals, objectives, and action items. 
One such objective is to increase capabilities by 
upgrading existing City-owned infrastructure to 
improve overall resilience. The City developed 
the associated action item to move Fire Station 
1 from its current unreinforced masonry building 
into a modern hazard-resistant self-contained 
structure and include a separate standalone 
Emergency Operations Center (EOC). The City 
will also construct Fire Station 8 in the Rancho 
Del Oro commercial area. Further, in order to 
reduce the possibility of damage and losses to life, 
property, and the environment, the City will hire 
a Community Risk Reduction Officer to develop 
a public awareness program that addresses fire 
resilient design, fuel modification, evacuation 
routes, and other preparedness measures as well 
as utilize aggressive vegetation management 
programs to provide buffer zones between unim-
proved wildland and development.

SAFE AND RESILIENT ENVIRONMENT 6
Urban Fire
An urban fire is a fire that can rapidly spread to 
adjoining structures and damage or destroy large 
commercial buildings, apartment complexes, and 
other residential or commercial facilities. Urban 
fires can also spread beyond the built environ-
ment and impact adjacent natural areas. As 
described above, much of the fire risk the City 
faces stems from the proximity of urban areas 
– primarily residential neighborhoods – to areas 
with high fire risk due to steep slopes, vegetation 
that can act as fuel for fires, and seasonal winds 
which can spread fire. The primary factors affect-
ing the risk of structural fire are the age and con-
dition of the building or structure, its proximity to 
other structures, and the methods and materials 
used in its construction. 
Urban fires usually result from sources within 
the structures themselves. Smoking in bed, 
faulty wiring, errant matches, and appliance mal-
functions are often causes of structural fires. 
Additionally, cinders from wood-burning fire-
places that remain alive and travel considerable 
distances have also been blamed for starting fires 
near residential locations. Therefore, urban fires 
can generally be mitigated through proper build-
ing code requirements, fire flow minimums, and 
zoning or subdivision ordinance requirements.
SOCIAL VULNERABILITY 
Oceanside is located in a semi-arid climate where 
wildfires and high temperatures are common, 
and such hazards are felt most acutely by front-
line communities. Neighborhoods that are more 
linguistically isolated are more likely to be at 
significant risk of wildfires. Linguistically isolat-
ed households (residents who do not speak or 
read English as a first language or at all) may not 
hear or understand important information when 
there is a fire or other emergency. According to 
American Community Survey estimates from 
2018, areas along the norther border of the city 
in close proximity to the WUI interface—including 
the South Morro Hills, North Valley, and East Side 
Capistrano neighborhoods—are more linguistical-
ly isolated than other areas of the city. Another 
population vulnerable to fire hazards are the 
City’s unhoused residents, many of whom live in 
isolated encampments in the San Luis Rey River.
Uncontrolled wildland fires do also have the risk of 
spreading beyond the very high and high vulner-
ability areas into urban areas, which could impact 
socially vulnerable populations. Additionally, the 
entire city will be impacted by wildfires occurring 
throughout the metropolitan region via impacts 
on air/wildfire smoke, water, and soil quality; 
damage to energy infrastructure and roads; and 
strain on local firefighting resources as the fire 
department is called to respond to fires across 
the region and State. Unhoused populations, out-
door workers, residents who live in poorly insu-
lated or ventilated homes, and people who are 
already burdened by elevated local (indoor/out-
door) pollution are increasingly at risk due to the 
consequences of climate change that have exac-
erbated the now-annual “smoke season.” Goals 
and policies developed by the City will work to 
mitigate fire hazards while prioritizing adaptation 
for socially vulnerable groups through compli-
ance with state laws, fire safe development regu-
lations, and local policies and programs.

INSTITUTIONAL AND REGULATORY 
FRAMEWORK 
Fire Safe Development Codes 
The California Fire Code (Title 24, Part 9 of the 
California Code) establishes regulations to pro-
tect life and property from the hazards of fires 
in new and existing buildings and structures. The 
provisions of the Fire Code apply to the construc-
tion, alteration, movement, enlargement, replace-
ment, repair, equipment, use and occupancy, 
location, maintenance, removal, and demolition 
of buildings or structures throughout California. 
Public Resources Code 4291 includes regulations 
and defensible space requirements for areas 
located in SRAs. The City adopted and amended 
the 2022 California Fire Code and regulates fire 
safety in Chapter 11 of the Oceanside Code of 
Ordinances (COD). In addition, Chapter 17 of the 
Oceanside COD establishes that any tree, plant, 
vine, or foliage that constitutes a danger to public 
safety by creating a fire hazard shall be consid-
ered a nuisance and must be abated.
Peakload Water Supply Requirement
The California Fire Code (Fire Code) stipulates 
fire-flow requirements for buildings.19 Fire-flow 
is the rate of a water supply, measured at 20 
pounds per square inch (psi) (138 kPa) residual 
pressure, that is available for firefighting. Fire-
flow minimums vary depending on building use, 
building size, and if a sprinkler system is provided. 
Water mains serving one- and two-family dwell-
ings, townhouses, and group homes must provide 
a fire-flow of 1,000 gallons per minute (gpm) for 
buildings without an automatic sprinkler system, 
or 500 gpm for buildings with fire protection 
devices such as automatic sprinkler systems. 
The required fire-flow standard for commercial, 
industrial, manufacturing, and large apartment 
buildings varies from 1,500 to 8,000 gpm based 
on the type of construction, type of use, and any 
built-in fire protection devices. School buildings 
are within Appendix BB of the Fire Code and 
range between 1,500 to 8,000 gpm depending 
on type and square footage. 
19 California Fire Code 2019, Appendix B Fire-Flow 
Requirements for Buildings. Table B105.1(1) and Table 
B105.1(2).
According to the City of Oceanside’s 2020 Urban 
Water Management Plan (UWMP), approximate-
ly 89 percent of the City’s water was purchased 
from the San Diego County Water Authority 
(SDCWA) in calendar year 2020. SDCWA sup-
plies are a combination of imported water from 
the State Water Project and Colorado River 
Aqueduct as well as desalinated seawater from 
the Claude “Bud” Lewis Carlsbad Desalination 
Plant. Approximately 10 percent of the City’s 
water comes from the Mission Basin, a ground-
water sub-basin that stores water classified as 
subsurface flows from the San Luis Rey River. 
The City also reclaims wastewater at the San 
Luis Rey Water Reclamation Facility (SLRWRF); 
this non-potable recycled water comprises 
approximately one percent of total water use. 
In addition, the City of Oceanside’s Pure Water 
Oceanside Project is the first advanced water 
treatment facility to become operational in the 
San Diego region and will purify recycled water 
to create a new, local source of drinking water. 
The City plans to produce 4.5 million gallons per 
day, enough to provide about 30 percent of their 
water supply. Under a second phase to the plan, 
the facility will expand to produce up to 6 million 
gallons per day, with non-potable recycled water 
anticipated to comprise approximately 24 per-
cent of total water use.
As detailed in the UWMP, the City’s water supply 
reliability analysis shows that with implementa-
tion of additional planned supplies and conserva-
tion measures, supplies will meet demand under 
all hydrologic scenarios, including the normal 
year, single dry year, and five consecutive dry 
years from 2025-2045. Concurrently with the 
2020 UWMP, the City developed the 2021 Water 
Conservation Master Plan Update (2021 WCMP 
Update). As part of this effort, the City project-
ed water use, passive conservation, and active 
conservation into the future. Moving forward, 
the City assumes implementation of aggressive 
water conservation, smart meters, and further 
implementation of recycled water conversions. 
Such conservation measures will allow the City 
to maintain an adequate water supply for fire 
suppression needs.
